android-app.p1: The zcrypt Android app is a beta build that runs the same zcrypt interface on your phone. Under the shell, encryption, compression, chunking, and storage sync run in zcrypt-core, the same in-process Rust engine that powers the desktop app, not a browser sandbox and not a background subprocess. Because the engine is the same, a file encrypted on desktop opens cleanly on Android, and vice versa.
android-app.p2: It is not on the Play Store. You install it by sideloading an APK directly, which takes about a minute.
android-app.p4: The APK is published alongside the other zcrypt builds. Grab it from the download page and install it yourself:
android-app.p5: Open <l1>the Android section of the download page</l1> on your phone and download the APK.
android-app.p6: When Android asks, allow installing from this source: sideloading an app from outside the Play Store needs that one-time permission.
android-app.p7: Open the downloaded APK to install, then launch zcrypt and sign in as you would anywhere else.
android-app.p8: Because it is sideloaded, the app does not auto-update through the Play Store. To move to a newer build, download and install the latest APK again from the same place.
android-app.p10: The Android app is genuinely early, and we would rather say so than oversell it. The encrypted drive works (sign in, upload, browse, and download) but the app is younger than the web and desktop builds, so expect rough edges and fewer conveniences for now. Offline access and camera backup are on the roadmap, not shipped.
android-app.p11: If a build for your phone gives you trouble, the <l1>web app</l1> runs the full product in your mobile browser in the meantime.
android-app.p13: The Android app is the same zcrypt, not a stripped-down sibling. Encryption and decryption happen entirely on your device, your vault passphrase is still never sent to the server, and everything you learn about how zcrypt protects your data applies here unchanged.
android-app.p14: Like the desktop app, Android uploads directly to your own storage: BYOS-direct: desktop and mobile upload straight to the user's own GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account using credentials from the OS keychain, so the backend never touches the platform token. The web app is the exception, because browser sandboxing blocks direct platform access, so it relays ciphertext through the backend.
android-app.p15: Because the cryptography is identical to every other platform, the recovery rules are too: lose your vault passphrase and your files cannot be decrypted on any device. Keep it in a password manager. See <l1>Account recovery</l1>.
android-app.p17: <l1>Desktop app: the same engine as a native build for your computer</l1>
android-app.p18: <l1>Web app: the full product in any modern browser</l1>
android-app.p20: <l1>zcrypt everywhere: one vault across web, desktop, and mobile</l1>

api.p1: Base URL. Your backend origin, with every route under /api. On a self-hosted instance this is whatever you set as BACKEND_URL.
api.p2: Content type. Request and response bodies are JSON, except chunk transfers, which send and receive raw bytes. JSON request bodies are capped at 1 MB.
api.p3: Errors. Non-2xx responses return '{' "error": "message" '}' with a matching HTTP status.
api.p4: Rate limits. Requests are rate-limited per IP. Auth and public (share / send / pad) routes have their own tighter limits; the SSE and WebSocket endpoints are exempt.
api.p5: This documents the routes the web, desktop, and Android apps use today. zcrypt is open source and pre-1.0. Treat the surface as evolving, and read RegisterRoutes in app/backend/cmd/server.go as the authoritative route table.
api.p8: Authenticate by sending a JSON Web Token in the Authorization header. Logging in returns an access token (and a refresh token); send the access token on every protected request.
api.p11: When an account has two-factor enabled, login returns a 2FA challenge instead of tokens; complete it with POST /api/auth/2fa/verify. Access tokens are short-lived. Use POST /api/auth/refresh to mint a new one.
api.p16: Sign in; returns tokens or a 2FA challenge.
api.p17: Exchange a refresh token for a new access token.
api.p19: Complete a TOTP challenge during login.
api.p23: Reset a password with a token.
api.p29: Files and folders carry only encrypted metadata. Folders can be nested, renamed, moved, and given their own password; deletes are soft (Trash) until purged. File names and folder names are ciphertext on the server.
api.p37: Move a file into a folder.
api.p47: Uploads are client-side encrypted and chunked. Initialise a session, push each encrypted chunk (or upload it directly to the platform via a presigned URL where supported), then complete the session. Sessions are resumable: query status and re-send only the chunks that are missing.
api.p51: Start an upload session; returns a session id. The body must carry encrypted_name, or the server answers 426 with code client_update_required. Files over 10 GiB get 413.
api.p52: Upload one encrypted chunk through the server.
api.p53: Get a presigned URL to upload a chunk directly.
api.p55: Finalise the file once all chunks are in.
api.p58: Chunk uploads carry an X-Chunk-SHA256 hash and an X-Chunk-Compressed flag so the server can verify each chunk and record how it was packed, without ever decrypting it.
api.p61: Downloads fetch metadata, then pull chunks by index. The client verifies each chunk, reassembles, decrypts with your passphrase-derived key, and decompresses, all locally.
api.p65: File metadata: size, chunk count, salt/IV.
api.p66: Batch metadata for up to 200 file ids in one request.
api.p67: Fetch one encrypted chunk by index.
api.p69: Share links expose a single file to anyone with the token, optionally guarded by a password and bounded by an expiry or download limit. The public read routes are unauthenticated and rate-limited; a share password is supplied via the X-Share-Password header.
api.p77: Public: file metadata for the share.
api.p80: A folder link publishes a set of files behind a single public token. The link key is generated on the client and lives only in the URL fragment, it is never sent to the server, and each file’s content key is re-wrapped under it, so the public routes only ever return opaque ciphertext. A link can carry a password (sent in the X-Share-Password header), an expiry, and a download cap. The public read routes are unauthenticated and rate-limited.
api.p87: Public: link info and the file listing.
api.p88: Public: one file's metadata + wrapped key.
api.p89: Public: fetch a chunk of a linked file.
api.p91: A shared vault (a “space”) lets several accounts share files under role-based access. The space has its own random key that the client seals to each member’s public key (see User keys below), and every shared file’s content key is re-wrapped under the space key. The server only ever stores these opaque grants, it can add, remove, and rotate them but never open them. Owners and admins manage members; only the owner can rotate the key or delete the space. Adding or removing files is limited to editors and admins.
api.p97: Space detail with members and files.
api.p99: Add a member with a sealed grant (owner or admin).
api.p100: Remove a member (owner or admin; only the owner can remove an admin). Members can remove themselves.
api.p101: Share a file into the space (editor/admin).
api.p102: Share many files into the space in one transaction (editor/admin). The free plan caps a batch at max_space_batch_files (default 200).
api.p104: Rotate the space key after a change (owner).
api.p105: Rotating re-seals a fresh space key to the remaining members and re-wraps every file’s key under it, so a removed member’s old grant, and any copy of the old key, can no longer open the space’s files.
api.a106: Rotation is what makes removal a revocation
api.p108: To seal a space key to another account, every user gets an X25519 keypair generated on the client. The private key is wrapped under your passphrase-derived key and stored only as ciphertext the server can’t read; the public key and a short fingerprint are stored in the clear so others can seal grants to you. These routes never return anyone else’s private key.
api.p112: Your key record (wrapped private key, wrapped master key if set, and the master_key_writes flag), or null.
api.p114: Resolve a user's public key by email or username (identifier query).
api.p115: Fetch another user's public key by id.
api.p117: Send lets anyone upload an encrypted file without an account and hand over a token; Pad stores a one-time encrypted note. Both are unauthenticated and rate-limited by IP.
api.p123: Finalise the send; returns a token.
api.p126: Read pad info, then its content.
api.p128: A timed vault groups files under a name and a countdown. The expiry is a label, not a delete trigger, deleting a vault never deletes the files it references. The expiry must be at least an hour out.
api.p137: Snapshots capture a point-in-time manifest of your file list; the integrity monitor records each file’s SHA-256 and size so a later check can flag a hash that changed. Both are metadata-only, no file contents are stored or restored. See <l1>Snapshots & integrity</l1>.
api.p146: Record a file's hash + size reference.
api.p147: Check a file against its latest reference.
api.p148: List files whose hash no longer matches.
api.p150: Offline pins mark files to keep available on a device; the encrypted clipboard syncs small snippets between your own devices. Clipboard items are encrypted on the client (the server stores only ciphertext, capped at 512 KB per item) and a push notifies your other devices over the event stream.
api.p155: Pin a file for offline access.
api.p157: Push an encrypted clipboard item (text / image / link).
api.p162: Sync folders are a per-device registry of local folders the desktop client keeps in sync. The server stores only the configuration and the stats a client reports back, the actual file syncing happens on your machine.
api.p169: Report sync results (file count, total size).
api.p172: Real-time progress (uploads, syncs) streams over Server-Sent Events. Because EventSource cannot set headers, first trade your access token for a single-use ticket, then open the stream with it. The ticket is valid for 30 seconds, so the token itself never appears in a URL or a proxy log.
api.p175: The stream carries upload and sync progress plus a clipboard event, emitted to your other connections when a new clipboard item is pushed. It closes when the access token it was opened with expires, or as soon as your sessions are revoked, so reconnect with a fresh ticket. Each account can hold a limited number of open streams. A separate WebSocket endpoint, GET /api/transfer/ws, backs live device-to-device transfer. Both long-lived endpoints bypass the per-request rate limiter.
api.p177: These routes report account limits, connected storage, and instance settings. Most are read-only for normal users; writing config requires admin.
api.p181: Storage quota and max concurrent uploads.
api.p186: List repositories in your storage pool.
api.p190: Admin routes require an account with the admin role. They cover user management, quotas and plans, global tokens, and audit data.
api.p196: Set a user's role. Send the acting admin's password, and a 2FA code if enabled.
api.p199: Delete a user. Needs the same re-authentication as a role change.
api.p202: Looking to run your own instance? See <l1>Self-hosting</l1> and <l2>Architecture</l2>.

api.description: zcrypt exposes a JSON REST API. Encryption happens on the client, so the API only ever moves opaque ciphertext, metadata, and chunks, never plaintext or keys.
api.p204: Edit the space name, description, or size limit (owner or admin).
api.p205: Change a member's role (owner or admin; only the owner can grant or change admin).
api.p206: Store your wrapped account master key (mk1). Set once: a second write returns 409.
api.p207: A user's avatar image. Visible to that user and to people who share a space with them; anyone else gets 404.
api.p208: The visitor's two-letter country code taken from edge headers, or an empty string (no auth).
api.p209: Turn master-key (mk1) writes on or off. Off by default; GET on the same path reads the current value.

architecture.p1: A file's life in zcrypt is: your browser splits it into chunks and compresses and encrypts each one; the chunks travel over a chunked HTTP API to the Go backend; the backend stages them on durable disk and a background worker syncs them to a storage platform you own; a PostgreSQL index records the ciphertext metadata that lets you find and reassemble the file later. Plaintext and keys never leave your device.
architecture.p6: Everything that makes a file private happens before it leaves your device, in this order:
architecture.p7: Chunk. The file is split into chunks sized to your device (4, 10, 16 or 32 MiB; 10 MiB is the usual). Chunking is what makes large files fast, parallel, and resumable. Each chunk is then processed on its own.
architecture.p8: Compress and encrypt. Each chunk is compressed with zstd (skipped when it would not shrink), then sealed with AES-256-GCM under a random per-file key. That key is wrapped by a key derived from your passphrase (PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations, with a unique per-file salt). Authenticated encryption means tampering is detectable on the way back.
architecture.p9: Hash. Each encrypted chunk is hashed with SHA-256, so the server and your storage can be checked against it without anything being decrypted.
architecture.p10: In the web app this pipeline runs in a pool of Web Workers, so compression, encryption, and hashing happen off the main thread and in parallel across CPU cores. Chunk buffers are handed to and from the workers by transfer (zero-copy, no duplicate allocation), and the pool size scales to the device’s cores and memory. The same worker pool runs the reverse pipeline on download.
architecture.p11: The same pipeline runs everywhere zcrypt runs: in the web app’s Web Worker pool, in zcrypt-core, the native Rust engine behind the desktop and Android apps, so a file uploaded from any one of them decrypts cleanly in the others.
architecture.p13: Downloads run the client pipeline in reverse. The app fetches each encrypted chunk, verifies its SHA-256, then decrypts and (where needed) decompresses it in the same Web Worker pool, so a large download parallelizes across cores instead of freezing the tab.
architecture.p14: Small files are reassembled in memory and saved as a download. A file too large to hold in a browser tab is instead streamed straight to disk: using the browser’s File System Access API, the app opens a writable to the file you pick, writes chunks in order as they are decrypted, and hashes them in write-order, so peak memory stays flat no matter how large the file. The whole-file hash is checked before the file is committed; an integrity mismatch or a cancel discards the partial file rather than leaving a corrupt one behind.
architecture.p15: Downloads are resumable within a session: a pause or a transient network failure keeps what has already been decrypted (or written to disk), so a later run continues from the high-water mark instead of restarting at chunk zero.
architecture.p17: The backend is plain Go standard-library net/http, no web framework. The client opens an upload session, then sends each encrypted chunk as raw bytes with a SHA-256 header the server uses to verify integrity (never to decrypt). Where a platform supports it, the client can request a presigned URL and upload a chunk straight to the platform, skipping the server relay. Downloads run the same path in reverse: metadata first, then chunks by index.
architecture.p18: Because uploads are session-based and chunk-addressed, they are inherently resumable, the client asks which chunks already landed and re-sends only the gaps.
architecture.p20: Uploaded chunks are not pushed to a storage platform inline. The server first writes each chunk to a durable staging directory on disk, which survives restarts. A background sync worker then drains that staging area, pushing chunks to the right platform repository and recording the result. This decouples the user-facing upload from the slower, retry-prone platform push.
architecture.p21: Resilience. If a platform push fails, the chunk stays staged and is retried; a crash mid-upload doesn't lose already-received chunks.
architecture.p22: Read-through. If you download a file whose chunks haven't been synced off staging yet, the server serves them straight from the staging directory.
architecture.p23: Progress. Upload and sync progress is pushed to the client over Server-Sent Events.
architecture.p24: This staging-and-relay path is how the web app moves chunks. The desktop and Android apps upload directly to your connected platform using credentials from your OS keychain, the backend only receives metadata (file ID, chunk index, platform, ciphertext hash), never the chunk bytes or your platform token. See Desktop app.
architecture.a25: Desktop and Android skip the relay
architecture.p27: Each storage backend implements a common adapter interface, upload, download, delete, create repo, list chunks, and report repo size, so the pipeline treats GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, and Telegram uniformly. Optional capabilities layer on top: some adapters batch many chunk uploads into a single commit, and some support direct presigned uploads.
architecture.p28: A repo pool sits in front of the adapters. Each file's chunks go to a single platform, and as a repository approaches that platform's size threshold the pool auto-rotates to a fresh repo. Once you connect your own account, your usable space is bounded by that account, not by a fixed cap. Until then, uploads use zcrypt's shared storage, which is capped at 1 GiB per account.
architecture.p29: Repositories, commit messages, and stored chunk file names are generated to look like ordinary developer activity, so the storage side reveals nothing about your real files. See <l1>Storage obfuscation</l1>.
architecture.p32: A PostgreSQL database, accessed through pgx with raw SQL (no ORM), is the index that ties everything together: users, folders and files, per-file salts and chunk references, encrypted platform tokens, shares, and more. Every record about a file is metadata or ciphertext: the database holds no readable file contents and no passphrase. The schema is applied automatically on startup.
architecture.p34: Sharing keeps the zero-knowledge boundary intact by moving keys, never plaintext. Every user has an X25519 keypair generated on their device; the private key is wrapped under their passphrase-derived key, so the server stores only ciphertext, while the public key and a short fingerprint are public so others can seal grants to them.
architecture.p35: A shared space (“shared vault”) has its own random symmetric key. To grant a member access, that space key is sealed to the member’s public key with an ECIES construction, an ephemeral X25519 key does ECDH with the recipient, and the shared secret is hashed into an AES-256-GCM wrapping key, and each shared file’s content key is re-wrapped under the space key. The server holds only these opaque grants: it can store, hand out, and delete them, but can never open one. Removing a member and rotating the space key re-seals a fresh key to the people who remain and re-wraps every file under it, so the old grant is dead.
architecture.p36: Public folder links work the same way: the link key is generated on the client and lives only in the URL fragment, and each file’s content key is re-wrapped under it, the server serving the link never sees the key.
architecture.p38: The line between your device and the server is the security boundary. Cross it, and only ciphertext and metadata exist:
architecture.p39: Your passphrase, and the key derived from it, never leave the client. They are never sent, stored, or logged.
architecture.p40: Chunks arrive already encrypted; the server verifies their hashes but cannot decrypt them.
architecture.p41: Platform tokens are the one secret the server does hold, and they're encrypted at rest with a per-user key derived from the instance MASTER_KEY via HKDF, so the storage platform never sees plaintext, and the database never sees a usable token.
architecture.p42: Because the server has nothing to decrypt your files with, neither do we, and neither does anyone who compromises the server. The flip side is that a forgotten passphrase is unrecoverable. See <l1>Zero-knowledge architecture</l1>.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.description: zcrypt is a thin, stateless server wrapped around a client-side encryption pipeline and your own storage accounts. Here is how the pieces connect, and why the server can never read your files.

authentication.p1: zcrypt uses two different secrets, and keeping them straight is the single most important thing to understand about your account.
authentication.p2: Your account password authenticates you to the service. It is sent to the server (over TLS), where it is verified against a bcrypt hash. Resetting it is routine.
authentication.p3: Your vault passphrase encrypts your files. It is used only on your device to derive your encryption keys and is never sent to the server. Because we never see it, we can never reset it for you. See Account recovery.
authentication.a4: These are not the same secret
authentication.p5: Everything on this page is about the first secret: how you sign in. For how the second secret protects your data, see <l1>Key management</l1>.
authentication.p7: Create an account with an email address, a username, and a password. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt before storage: the server never keeps your password in plaintext. To be accepted, a password must meet a basic complexity bar:
authentication.p11: At least one special character (anything that isn't a letter or number)
authentication.p12: No longer than 72 bytes, bcrypt's input limit (72 plain letters, fewer with accents or emoji)
authentication.p13: zcrypt also checks your chosen password against the HaveIBeenPwned breach corpus using a k-anonymity range query: only the first five characters of a SHA-1 hash leave your session, never the password itself. If the password has appeared in a known breach, you get a warning with the breach count and can choose a stronger one or proceed anyway. The same check runs when you set a new password during a reset.
authentication.p14: A breach warning never silently blocks you. It is advice. The check also fails open: if the breach service is unreachable, sign-up is not held up.
authentication.p16: When email is configured for your instance, signing up sends a verification link to your address. Verifying your email protects you in one concrete way: a verified email is required before an OAuth provider with the same address can be auto-linked to your account, so nobody can attach their Google or GitHub identity to an email you have not proven you control. You can request a fresh verification link if the first one expires.
authentication.p18: Prefer not to type a password? Request a magic link and zcrypt emails you a one-time sign-in link. Opening it logs you in and, if your email wasn't verified yet, verifies it at the same time. Magic links are single-use and short-lived, so an old link in your inbox can't be replayed later.
authentication.p19: To resist account enumeration, the “login link sent” response looks identical whether or not an account exists for that address. Only the real owner of the inbox ever receives a working link.
authentication.p21: Forgot your account password? Request a reset and follow the link emailed to you to choose a new one. New passwords must pass the same complexity and breach checks as sign-up. Completing a reset is a hard security boundary:
authentication.p22: Your token version is bumped, which invalidates every existing access token immediately.
authentication.p23: All refresh tokens are deleted, so every signed-in device is forced to log in again.
authentication.p24: Resetting your account password restores access to the service. It does not, and cannot, decrypt your vault. Your files stay sealed under your vault passphrase, which the reset flow never sees.
authentication.a25: A password reset does not touch your files
authentication.p27: After you sign in, zcrypt issues two tokens. A short-lived access token (a signed JWT) authorizes your API requests, and a longer-lived refresh token is exchanged silently in the background for a fresh access token so you stay signed in without re-entering your password.
authentication.p37: Refresh tokens are stored only as hashes on the server and are rotated on every use, so a captured refresh token has a short useful life. Access-token JWTs are signed with HS256 and pin their type, so a token minted for one purpose (for example the mid-login 2FA step) can never be replayed as a full session token.
authentication.p38: Each JWT carries a token version. Bumping your token version invalidates every outstanding access token at once and clears your refresh tokens, an instant “sign out of all sessions”. A password reset does exactly this for you.
authentication.p41: For a second layer on sign-in, enable time-based one-time-password (TOTP) two-factor authentication. It works with any standard authenticator app. Google Authenticator, 1Password, Aegis, Authy, and others: using the usual 6-digit, 30-second codes.
authentication.p42: Start setup in your account settings. zcrypt generates a secret and an otpauth:// URI you scan as a QR code (or enter by hand).
authentication.p43: Enter a current 6-digit code from your authenticator to confirm the secret synced correctly. Only then is 2FA switched on.
authentication.p44: From then on, signing in asks for a code. Your password is checked first; only on success does the server hand back a short-lived temporary token to complete the 2FA step.
authentication.p45: When you enable 2FA, zcrypt also issues a set of one-time backup codes. Save them somewhere safe, if you lose your authenticator, a backup code gets you back in. Each code works once, and you can regenerate a fresh set at any time, which invalidates the old ones.
authentication.p46: To turn 2FA off, you must confirm both your current password and a valid code, so a stranger who briefly has your unlocked session still can't strip the second factor. Code validation allows a one-step time window on either side to tolerate minor clock drift between your phone and the server.
authentication.p47: TOTP guards the front door to your account. It is independent of your vault passphrase: even with a valid code, your files remain encrypted until you unlock the vault on your device.

bulk.p1: Multi-select is built into the explorer. Use your mouse to pick out files, and the usual keyboard modifiers to extend a selection. Add individual files, or select a contiguous range: then keep going with the keyboard to grow or shrink it. The toolbar updates to show how many items are selected and which bulk actions apply.
bulk.p3: With several files selected, download them together as a single ZIP archive. Each file is fetched, verified, decrypted, and decompressed on your device, exactly like a normal download, and then packed into the ZIP locally. Nothing is ever assembled or decrypted on the server. Files from protected folders are decrypted with their folder password as part of the same pass.
bulk.p4: ZIP creation happens in your browser, so it has limits. A ZIP can hold at most 65,535 files and 4 GiB in total, and a single file over 1 GiB cannot go in a ZIP, so download it on its own. A browser that cannot stream to disk (such as Safari or Firefox) must build the archive in memory and is also capped at about 2 GB; Chromium browsers can stream it to disk instead. The desktop app builds ZIPs natively and does not have these browser limits.
bulk.p7: Select a batch and delete it in one action. Like single deletes, this moves the files to the <l1>Trash</l1>, where they can be restored or purged later, so a bulk delete is recoverable until you empty the Trash.

bulk.description: Act on many files at once: select a batch and download it as a single ZIP, or move it to the Trash together. Selection works the way you expect with both mouse and keyboard.

concepts.p1: Your vault is your encrypted drive: the entire tree of folders and files that belong to you. It is presented like any normal drive, but every name and every byte inside it is encrypted on your device before it is stored. The server holds only ciphertext and the structure needed to fetch it back.
concepts.p3: Your passphrase is the one secret that unlocks the vault. It is not a login credential: your account password handles signing in. Instead, zcrypt feeds the passphrase through a key derivation function in your browser to produce your vault key. That key, and the passphrase behind it, are never transmitted to our servers.
concepts.p4: Because nothing readable leaves your device, a forgotten passphrase cannot be reset. There is nothing on our side to recover it from. Store it in a password manager. See <l1>Passphrase & key management</l1> for the derivation details.
concepts.p7: Folders are real and nestable, just like on a desktop drive. Open one and create another inside it, as deep as you like. A folder's name is encrypted on your device exactly like file contents, so your organization is private too. When the vault is locked, names show as placeholders until you unlock.
concepts.p8: A folder can also have its own password layered on top. See <l1>Per-folder encryption</l1>.
concepts.p10: zcrypt uses envelope encryption. Each file gets its own random content encryption key (CEK) that encrypts that file's bytes with AES-256-GCM. The CEK itself is then encrypted (“wrapped”) by the key derived from your passphrase.
concepts.p11: The payoff: your passphrase only ever has to protect small wrapped keys, not gigabytes of data. To open a file, zcrypt unwraps its CEK with your vault key, then uses the CEK to decrypt the content, all locally.
concepts.p13: Each file is split into chunks first: pieces sized to your device (4, 10, 16 or 32 MiB; 10 MiB is the usual). Each chunk is then compressed and encrypted on its own. Chunks are what actually get uploaded, one per request, to the repositories or channel on your connected platform. On download, zcrypt fetches the chunks, verifies them, and reassembles the file on your device.
concepts.p15: The vault has a single lock state, surfaced as one pill in the interface and unlocked through one modal. Enter your passphrase once and the whole vault unlocks for the rest of the session. There is no per-file or per-folder prompting to wade through.
concepts.p16: The unlock lasts for a session time-to-live (TTL). When it expires, the pill returns to locked and the next action that needs your key reopens the single modal.
concepts.p18: When unlocking, you can choose “keep me unlocked on this device.” Instead of re-typing your passphrase every session, zcrypt stores it encrypted at rest in your browser's IndexedDB, sealed under a non-extractable key the browser will not hand back to any script.
concepts.p29: This is meaningfully harder to scrape than a passphrase sitting in localStorage, and it is never sent to the server. It still trusts the device, so only enable it on hardware you control. Locking the vault or signing out clears it.
concepts.a30: Safer than localStorage, but still local trust
concepts.title: Core concepts
concepts.description: A few ideas explain almost everything about how zcrypt works. Understand these and the rest of the product reads itself.

connect-storage.p1: zcrypt is free and open source and does not run a storage farm. Your encrypted chunks live inside a platform account you connect, which means your capacity is simply the free space that platform gives you. Today zcrypt supports GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, and Telegram.
connect-storage.p3: Open Settings and go to the platforms section. Add the platform you want, paste its token, and save. You can connect more than one: adding a second backend simply adds its free space to your total.
connect-storage.p5: At a high level, each platform needs a credential that lets zcrypt create private storage and read and write to it on your behalf. You generate these in the platform's own settings and paste them into zcrypt:
connect-storage.p9: A personal access token with private-repository access
connect-storage.p11: A personal access token with project read/write scope
connect-storage.p13: An access token that can create and write to private repos
connect-storage.p15: A bot token plus a private channel for the bot to post to
connect-storage.p16: The exact scopes and step-by-step instructions for each platform live in <l1>Bring your own storage</l1>.
connect-storage.p18: The platform tokens you save are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM before they are stored. They are not kept as plain text in our database. zcrypt uses them only to move your already encrypted chunks to and from your backend.
connect-storage.p19: Grant each token only the access zcrypt needs, and revoke it from the platform's own settings at any time to instantly cut zcrypt off from that backend.
connect-storage.p22: You never manage repositories by hand. zcrypt auto-creates private repositories (or uses your Telegram channel) and, as one fills toward its platform's limit, rotates to a fresh one automatically. Your usable space grows on its own as you upload.
connect-storage.p23: New repositories are created on demand, no setup step for you.
connect-storage.p24: When a repository nears its platform's size threshold, zcrypt moves new chunks to the next one.
connect-storage.p25: Connecting an additional platform expands the pool further.
connect-storage.p27: <l1>Bring your own storage: per-platform setup and token scopes</l1>
connect-storage.p28: <l1>Repo pool & rotation: how storage grows across repositories</l1>
connect-storage.title: Connect your storage
connect-storage.description: zcrypt doesn't sell you storage: you bring an account you already have. Connect a backend once and your encrypted files live there, under your control.

contributing.p1: zcrypt is a zero-knowledge encrypted cloud storage system, and this page mirrors the repository's CONTRIBUTING.md. Because it's a security/cryptography product, read docs/SECURITY.md before reporting anything that might be a vulnerability. Report it privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting (the repository's Security tab), and do not open a public issue for security problems.
contributing.p15: Never commit a real .env; it is gitignored. The backend template lives at app/backend/.env.example. Copy it to .env and supply your own values. Each contributor is responsible for their own credentials. If you accidentally commit a secret, rotate it immediately and let a maintainer know.
contributing.p17: Backend. Standard Go. stdlib net/http (no web framework). Wrap errors with fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err). UUID primary keys. Raw SQL via pgxpool (no ORM). Run go vet ./... and go test ./... before pushing.
contributing.p18: Frontend. TypeScript + React 19. "use client" for interactive components. Zustand for global state, Tailwind for styling, Hugeicons for icons. No emojis in code. Run bun run lint and bun run typecheck before pushing.
contributing.p19: Commits. Keep them focused and write clear messages.
contributing.p21: Before pushing, run the change-scoped quality gate. It runs typecheck, lint, tests, and build for whichever modules you touched (frontend / backend / core / desktop), mirroring CI:
contributing.p24: Once installed, the pre-push hook runs the gates automatically on git push; bypass a single push with git push --no-verify if you must.
contributing.a25: The pre-push hook runs this for you
contributing.p27: Fork the repository (or create a feature branch if you have write access). Do not commit directly to main.
contributing.p28: Use a descriptive branch name, e.g. feat/repo-rotation, fix/cors-whitelist, or docs/readme.
contributing.p29: Make your change with tests where it makes sense, and ensure the build, lint, type check, and tests pass.
contributing.p30: Open a pull request against main with a clear description of what changed and why. Link any related issue.
contributing.p31: A maintainer will review. Address feedback by pushing additional commits to the same branch.
contributing.p33: By contributing to zcrypt, you agree that your contributions will be licensed under the <l1>MIT License</l1>, the same license that covers the project.
contributing.title: Contributing
contributing.description: How to set up zcrypt locally, the conventions the project follows, and how to submit a change.

dead-mans-switch.p1: A dead man’s switch fires when you stop doing something. Here, that something is signing in. You nominate a trusted contact and a timeout; if you don’t check in before the timeout elapses, zcrypt sends that contact an email.
dead-mans-switch.p3: From settings, configure the switch with:
dead-mans-switch.p4: Contact email, who gets notified. A contact name is optional.
dead-mans-switch.p5: Timeout: anywhere from 7 to 365 days of inactivity before it fires.
dead-mans-switch.p6: A message: optional text included in the email to your contact. It is not end-to-end encrypted: the server and the email provider can read it, so do not put secrets in it.
dead-mans-switch.p7: You can enable, disable, or delete the switch at any time.
dead-mans-switch.p9: Every login counts as a check-in and resets the timer. As long as you keep signing in within your chosen window, the switch never fires. So the practical rule is simple: log in at least once per timeout period to stay silent.
dead-mans-switch.p11: The dead man’s switch sends a notification email to your contact. That is all it does.
dead-mans-switch.p12: It does not deliver your files, and it does not hand over any keys, because zcrypt is zero-knowledge, there are no keys on our side to give anyone. We cannot decrypt your vault, so the switch cannot pass your data to your contact.
dead-mans-switch.p13: There is an “include files” option, but it only changes the wording of the email. It does not attach, transfer, list, or unlock anything. If you want a contact to be able to reach your actual files, you must arrange that yourself (for example, by sharing a passphrase through your own trusted channel).
dead-mans-switch.a14: Read this before you rely on it
dead-mans-switch.p16: <l1>Decoy profile: a second password that opens a fake vault</l1>
dead-mans-switch.p17: <l1>Account recovery: what is and isn’t recoverable, and why</l1>
dead-mans-switch.title: Dead man's switch
dead-mans-switch.description: A safeguard that watches for your absence. If you stop checking in for a period you choose, zcrypt sends a message to a contact you trust: a way to make sure someone is alerted if something happens to you.

decoy-profile.p1: Your account can hold two passwords. Your real one unlocks your real vault. A separate decoy password unlocks a decoy vault, a self-contained space populated with fake files you control. To anyone watching you log in, the decoy looks like an ordinary, fully populated account.
decoy-profile.p2: This is sometimes called plausible deniability: when handing over a password is unavoidable, you can hand over one that opens something harmless.
decoy-profile.p4: In settings, set a decoy password. A few rules keep it credible:
decoy-profile.p5: It must be at least 6 characters.
decoy-profile.p6: It must differ from your real password: zcrypt rejects a match so the two vaults stay distinct.
decoy-profile.p7: You can enable or disable the decoy without deleting it, and remove it entirely whenever you like.
decoy-profile.p9: A decoy is only convincing if it looks lived-in, so you add fake files to it: each with a name and a size. These are placeholders that populate the listing to make the decoy vault look like a real one at a glance; they exist to furnish the disguise, not to be opened and read like your real files. Aim for a believable spread of names and sizes : a single test file gives the game away.
decoy-profile.p11: At the normal login screen, entering the decoy password signs you into the decoy vault instead of your real one. There’s no separate button or toggle that hints a second vault exists: the password you type decides which vault opens.
decoy-profile.p13: A decoy protects against someone who makes you reveal a password and glances at the result. It is not a defense against deep forensic analysis, traffic inspection, or an adversary who already knows zcrypt supports decoys and insists on more. Make the decoy genuinely believable, and remember that whether to use one at all, and what happens if you’re caught doing so: is a judgment call for your specific situation and jurisdiction.

decoy-profile.title: Decoy profile
decoy-profile.description: A second password that opens a believable, innocent-looking vault instead of your real one. If you're ever pressured (at a border, in a search, under coercion) you can unlock something that looks complete without exposing what actually matters.

desktop-app.p1: The zcrypt desktop app is a native build for macOS, Windows, and Linux, packaged with Tauri. Tauri renders the same zcrypt interface in a lightweight native shell using your operating system's own webview, so you get a proper application window and OS integration without a heavy bundled browser.
desktop-app.p2: Underneath that shell, encryption, compression, chunking, and storage sync run in zcrypt-core, an in-process Rust engine, not a browser sandbox and not a background subprocess. The same engine backs the Android app, so a file encrypted on desktop opens cleanly there too.
desktop-app.p4: Running natively unlocks a few things a browser tab can't do as cleanly:
desktop-app.p5: Native file picker: choose files and folders to upload through your operating system's own dialog.
desktop-app.p6: OAuth via your system browser: signing in with Google or GitHub opens your default browser rather than an embedded webview, so you authenticate in a trusted, familiar environment and the app receives your tokens through a one-time, single-use hand-off. See Sign in with Google or GitHub.
desktop-app.p7: A dedicated app window that lives in your dock or taskbar, separate from your browsing.
desktop-app.p9: The desktop app is the same zcrypt, not a stripped-down sibling. Encryption and decryption still happen entirely on your device, your vault passphrase is still never sent to the server, and the session vault lock behaves just as it does on the web. Anything you learn about how zcrypt protects your data applies here unchanged.
desktop-app.p10: One thing does differ: BYOS-direct: desktop and mobile upload straight to the user's own GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account using credentials from the OS keychain, so the backend never touches the platform token. The web app is the exception, because browser sandboxing blocks direct platform access, so it relays ciphertext through the backend.
desktop-app.p11: Because the cryptography is identical to the web app, the recovery rules are too: lose your vault passphrase and your files cannot be decrypted on any platform. Keep it in a password manager. See <l1>Account recovery</l1>.
desktop-app.p13: Desktop builds are published on the project's GitHub releases page. Grab the asset that matches your platform from there:
desktop-app.p14: <l1>zcrypt.cloud/download</l1> . Pick the latest release and download the build for macOS, Windows, or Linux.
desktop-app.p15: Or install from a terminal. These installers are unsigned (the macOS build is not notarized, and Windows signing only turns on once it is configured), and the scripts skip the first-launch "unverified app" prompt for you:
desktop-app.p22: If you installed a downloaded file by hand, the first launch may be blocked. On macOS, open System Settings, then Privacy & Security, and choose Open Anyway. On Windows, choose More info, then Run anyway in the SmartScreen prompt.
desktop-app.p24: The desktop app is young and ships from GitHub releases, so installers and platforms can vary between versions. The Linux build is x86_64 only. If you don't see a build for your OS yet, the <l1>web app</l1> gives you the full product in the meantime.
desktop-app.p26: <l1>Web app: the same product in any modern browser</l1>
desktop-app.p27: <l1>Android app: the same engine, sideloaded on your phone</l1>
desktop-app.p28: <l1>Sign in with Google or GitHub: including the desktop sign-in flow</l1>

downloading.p1: The server's only role in a download is to hand back the encrypted chunks it stored (or fetch them from your storage platform on your behalf). Every step that turns those chunks back into a readable file (decryption, decompression, verification) runs locally. The server never sees a decrypted byte and never sees your passphrase.
downloading.p2: The heavy work runs in a pool of Web Workers, off the main thread, so the app stays responsive while it decrypts: even on a multi-gigabyte file. The size of that pool is chosen from your device's CPU and memory rather than being fixed.
downloading.p4: Fetch. The browser requests the file's encrypted chunks, pulling several in parallel for speed. A dropped connection or slow chunk is retried on its own, and the access token is refreshed mid-download so a long transfer doesn't stall on an expired session.
downloading.p5: Decrypt & decompress. Each chunk is decrypted with AES-256-GCM using the per-file key unwrapped from your passphrase (or the folder password, for a protected folder), then decompressed with zstd: both in the worker pool, off the main thread.
downloading.p6: Verify. Once the chunks are reassembled, the file's SHA-256 is compared against the hash recorded at upload. A mismatch fails the download rather than saving a damaged file.
downloading.p7: Save. Small files are rebuilt in memory and downloaded the usual way; large files are streamed straight to disk as they arrive (below).
downloading.p9: For most files the browser rebuilds the whole thing in memory and then saves it. That approach breaks down once a file is larger than a browser tab can comfortably hold, so past roughly a gigabyte, zcrypt streams the download straight to disk instead. You choose where to save it up front (a Save-As prompt), and each chunk is decrypted and written out in order as it arrives, so the whole file never has to sit in RAM at once. This is what makes downloading very large files: on the order of tens of gigabytes, a 25 GB file, say, possible at all.
downloading.p10: Even the integrity hash is computed incrementally, as each chunk is written, so there's no second full-file copy made just to verify it. Dropping that duplicate buffer roughly halves peak memory versus assembling the whole file and then hashing it.
downloading.p12: Streaming to disk uses the browser's File System Access API, which today means a Chromium-based browser; where it isn't available, zcrypt falls back to the in-memory path. If a streamed download fails its integrity check or you cancel it, the partial file on disk is discarded: a corrupt or truncated file is never left committed.
downloading.p14: A download can be paused and picked back up: pausing keeps everything decrypted so far (and, for a large download streaming to disk, the open file on disk), and resuming continues from there instead of restarting at chunk zero. A retry after a failure does the same, it continues from what's already done rather than re-fetching the whole file. Pausing is deliberately distinct from stopping: a stop discards the in-progress work, a pause preserves it.
downloading.p15: Transient blips are handled for you. A dropped connection, a stalled chunk, or a temporary server error is retried automatically with backoff: on single-file downloads, on <l1>bulk ZIP downloads</l1>, and on shared-link downloads, so one hiccup over a long transfer doesn't sink the whole file.
downloading.p16: A download's partly-decrypted data lives on your device, so closing the tab restarts it from the beginning. This is the opposite of <l1>uploads</l1>, whose partial state is held on the server and survives a reload. See the <l2>transfer manager</l2> for the pause / resume / retry controls.
downloading.p19: Two things guard integrity. First, AES-256-GCM is an authenticated cipher, so a chunk that was altered in storage fails to decrypt rather than producing garbage: a tampered piece is caught the moment it is opened. Second, once every chunk is decrypted and reassembled, the file's SHA-256 is checked against the hash recorded at upload; a mismatch fails the download instead of saving a damaged file. On a streamed download that hash is built up as chunks are written, so the check costs no extra copy of the file.
downloading.p20: If the wrong passphrase or folder password is used, decryption fails outright instead of yielding a damaged file: the authenticated cipher simply will not open without the correct key.
downloading.p23: A file stored inside a <l1>password-protected folder</l1> is encrypted under that folder's password, not your vault passphrase. Downloading one prompts for the folder password (if the folder isn't already unlocked in this session), and that password is what unwraps the key locally. An unlocked vault alone is not enough to open a protected folder's files.

downloading.p26: <l1>Bulk operations: download many files at once as a ZIP</l1>

downloading.description: Getting a file back is the upload pipeline in reverse. Your browser pulls the encrypted chunks, decrypts them, and rebuilds the original, and the plaintext is reconstructed only on your device.

faq.p1: zcrypt is free and open source. There are no paid plans. You connect your own storage account, so once you do, your available space is bounded only by that platform's free space, not by us. Every line of code is public, so you can verify what it does rather than take our word for it.
faq.p3: You bring your own storage (BYOB). Connect a GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account and your capacity is whatever free space that platform gives you. zcrypt handles the compression, encryption, and chunking on top of it, and rotates across repositories as they fill, so you keep growing without hitting an artificial cap. Before you connect anything, new accounts can use 1 GiB of shared storage, and a single file can be up to 10 GiB.
faq.a4: How much storage do I get?
faq.p5: Files are sealed with AES-256-GCM, an authenticated encryption standard, before they leave your device. The key is derived locally from your passphrase and is never transmitted. This zero-knowledge design means even we cannot read your files, and neither can your storage platform, which only ever receives encrypted chunks.
faq.p7: Yes. Sign in to zcrypt from any modern browser or app, enter your passphrase, and your encrypted files are there. Everything is decrypted locally on whichever device you're using: the plaintext is never reconstructed on our servers.
faq.a8: Can I access my files across multiple devices?
faq.p9: Real folders. zcrypt is a full encrypted drive: create and nest folders, drag files to organize them, search, sort, and switch between grid and list views. Folder names are encrypted too, so even your structure stays private. See <l1>Folders & the file explorer</l1>.
faq.a10: Does zcrypt have real folders, or just a flat list?
faq.p11: Yes. zcrypt previews images, video, audio, PDFs, documents (DOCX), Markdown, CSVs, and source code directly in the browser. Each file is decrypted on the fly on your device: the plaintext never touches our servers. See <l1>Viewing & previewing files</l1>.
faq.a12: Can I preview files without downloading them?
faq.p13: Yes. Any folder can have its own password, separate from your account passphrase. The files inside are re-encrypted under that folder's key, so even with your vault unlocked, a protected folder stays sealed until you enter its password. See <l1>Per-folder encryption</l1>.
faq.a14: Can I password-protect a single folder?
faq.p15: Because zcrypt is strictly zero-knowledge, your passphrase is never stored on our servers and key derivation is one-way. If you lose it, your encrypted files cannot be recovered: by us or anyone else. There is no reset link for the passphrase itself, by design.
faq.p16: Store your passphrase in a password manager. It is the one secret that unlocks everything, and the one thing we genuinely cannot help you recover.
faq.a18: What happens if I forget my passphrase?
faq.title: FAQ
faq.description: Short, honest answers to the questions people ask most about zcrypt.

folder-encryption.p1: By default, every file in your vault is protected by your vault passphrase. Per-folder encryption adds an independent password to a specific folder, so opening that folder requires something extra: useful for the handful of folders you want sealed off even from your own everyday session.
folder-encryption.p2: There is no new cryptography here. A protected folder reuses the exact envelope encryption scheme used everywhere else in zcrypt. The only thing that changes is which password derives the key that wraps each file's Content Encryption Key, the folder password instead of the vault passphrase.
folder-encryption.p4: When you set a folder password, your device generates a random salt and builds a small verifier: a fixed constant encrypted with the folder-password-derived key. To check a typed password later, the client re-derives the key and tries to decrypt that verifier. The right password decrypts it; a wrong one fails GCM authentication. All of this happens on-device with no server round-trip.
folder-encryption.p7: The verifier lets the app tell you immediately whether a password is correct without decrypting a real file and without the server ever participating in the check. The server cannot validate the password because it never has the material to.
folder-encryption.a8: Why a verifier instead of asking the server
folder-encryption.p10: A file's already-uploaded chunks never get re-encrypted when you protect a folder. That would mean re-uploading everything. Instead, only the tiny wrapped key changes. When a file enters a protected folder, the client recovers its existing CEK under the source key, then re-wraps that same CEK under a fresh folder-password-derived key and a new salt.
folder-encryption.p11: Recover the file's existing CEK using the source password (vault passphrase or the old folder password).
folder-encryption.p12: Re-wrap that same CEK under the destination password's derived key with a new per-file salt.
folder-encryption.p13: Persist the new salt and wrapped CEK via the /rekey endpoint: it updates only those two fields and touches no chunk data.
folder-encryption.p14: Moving a file out of a protected folder runs the same dance in reverse, re-wrapping the CEK back under your vault passphrase. The underlying ciphertext on your storage backend is never rewritten.
folder-encryption.p16: For a protected folder, the server holds exactly two opaque, client-computed base64 blobs, and nothing else about the password:
folder-encryption.p17: pw_salt: the random per-folder salt used to derive the folder-password key on your device.
folder-encryption.p18: pw_verifier: the small ciphertext used for local verification. It reveals nothing about the password.
folder-encryption.p19: The server never derives, sees, or logs the folder password or any key derived from it. A folder counts as “protected” purely because pw_salt is present. Audit events for setting or clearing a folder password record only the folder ID, never the salt, the verifier, or any key material.
folder-encryption.a20: The folder password is never sent
folder-encryption.p22: A forgotten folder password is unrecoverable. Just like the vault passphrase, there is no reset: the key exists nowhere we can reach. Store it in a password manager.
folder-encryption.p23: It protects file contents, not the folder name in transit. Folder names are already encrypted client-side under your vault key; the folder password governs the files' content keys.
folder-encryption.p24: You must re-key before unprotecting. Removing a folder password requires the client to first re-key its files back to the vault passphrase, so nothing is left wrapped under a key you're about to discard.

folder-encryption.description: A folder can have its own password, separate from your vault passphrase: a second lock for the things that need one. It is built entirely on the same envelope primitive, and the folder password never leaves your device.

toc.key-in-fragment: The key lives in the link

folder-sharing.p1: From a folder in your vault, choose Share to mint a public link that covers the whole folder’s contents, including its sub-folders. zcrypt generates a random folder-share key in your browser and re-wraps each file’s content-encryption key under it, so recipients can decrypt without ever knowing your passphrase.
folder-sharing.p2: Your vault has to be unlocked to create the link, because zcrypt needs your passphrase locally to recover each file’s key and re-wrap it. Files that can’t be re-wrapped are simply left out and the rest are still shared, the dialog tells you how many files were shared and how many were skipped.
folder-sharing.p3: A file is skipped if it was uploaded before per-file sharing existed (no key envelope to re-wrap) or if it lives inside a password-protected folder (its key is sealed under that folder’s password, not your vault passphrase). If none of a folder’s files can be shared, zcrypt tells you rather than creating an empty link.
folder-sharing.p6: A folder link works exactly like a <l1>single-file share link</l1>, just for many files at once. The link has two parts that do very different jobs:
folder-sharing.p8: Everything after the # is the URL fragment. Browsers never transmit the fragment to the server, so the folder-share key stays in the address bar and is only readable by JavaScript on the page. Our servers store only the token and, per file, an opaque wrapped key they can never unwrap, never the folder key itself, and never any plaintext.
folder-sharing.p9: Anyone with the full link can open the folder, because the link carries the key. Send it over a channel you trust, and add a separate password (below) when the link might travel over something you don’t.
folder-sharing.a10: Treat the link like the folder's password
folder-sharing.a11: The key lives in the link, not on our servers
folder-sharing.p12: You can require a password on the link. It is hashed with bcrypt on the server and checked before anything about the folder’s contents is released. Until the correct password is supplied, the link won’t reveal the file listing at all, no names, no sizes, and no per-file keys. Only once the password checks out does the server hand back the list of files.
folder-sharing.p13: The password gates the listing on our side; the folder-share key in the fragment is what actually decrypts the files in the recipient’s browser. Someone needs both the full link and the password to open a protected folder.
folder-sharing.a14: The password and the key are two separate locks
folder-sharing.p16: Recipients need no zcrypt account. Opening the link loads a public page that lists the folder’s files and lets them download any one file or grab them all. It is read-only: a folder link is for handing files out, not for collaboration, no one can add, rename, or delete anything through it.
folder-sharing.p17: If the link is password-protected, the page prompts for the password first and only then shows the file listing.
folder-sharing.p18: Each download fetches the encrypted chunks, decrypts them entirely in the recipient’s browser using the key from the fragment, and verifies the file’s SHA-256 before saving it. Plaintext is reassembled on their device, never on our servers.
folder-sharing.p19: If the link has expired or hit its download limit, the page explains that it is no longer available.
folder-sharing.p21: Every folder link carries the same optional guardrails as a single-file share, all enforced on our side independently of the key in the fragment:
folder-sharing.p25: Choose 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or never. After it lapses the link reports that it is no longer available.
folder-sharing.p27: Cap the number of accesses (for example 10, 50, 100, or unlimited). Once the count reaches the cap, the link stops working, see the note below on how it counts.
folder-sharing.p29: Revoke any link at any time from the folder’s share dialog. Revocation is immediate: the server refuses all further requests for that token, so even someone holding the full link can no longer fetch the files.
folder-sharing.p31: A folder link and a <l1>shared vault</l1> solve different problems. Reach for the one that matches how much control you need:
folder-sharing.p35: Anyone with the link (plus the password, if set)
folder-sharing.p39: Role-based, members can be given write access
folder-sharing.p44: Handing a set of files to someone once
folder-sharing.p45: Ongoing collaboration on a shared set of files
folder-sharing.p47: The download counter increments each time a recipient’s browser fetches an individual file’s metadata, the step right before that file’s chunks download. So one “Download all” of a five-file folder counts as five, not one. If you set a tight max downloads, size it against the number of files in the folder, not the number of people you expect to open the link.
folder-sharing.a48: The cap counts files, not folder-opens
folder-sharing.p50: Other ways to get data to people and devices:
folder-sharing.p51: <l1>Share links, hand a single file to someone with a link</l1>
folder-sharing.p52: <l1>Shared vaults, collaborative vaults with named members and roles</l1>
folder-sharing.p53: <l1>Anonymous Send, send a file with no account at all</l1>
folder-sharing.title: Share a folder
folder-sharing.description: Hand someone a whole folder with one public link. Anyone with the link can browse and download the files read-only, no account required, and it stays zero-knowledge, because the folder's decryption key rides in the part of the URL that never reaches our servers.

folders.p1: From anywhere in your vault, use New folder to create a folder in the current location. Folders can be nested as deeply as you like. Open a folder and create another inside it. Folders always sort ahead of files so structure stays easy to scan.
folders.p2: Rename a folder at any time: the new name is re-encrypted on your device.
folders.p3: Delete a folder to move it (and its contents) to the Trash, where it can be restored or purged later.
folders.p4: Drop one file directly onto another to spin up a new folder containing both, handy for grouping on the fly.
folders.p6: The breadcrumb trail at the top of the explorer always shows where you are, starting from My Vault. Click any crumb to jump back up the tree. Breadcrumbs are also drop targets: drag a file or folder onto a crumb to move it to that level.
folders.p8: Switch between a grid of thumbnail cards and a sortable list. In list view, click a column header to sort by name, type, size, modified date, or Saved: how much space compression reclaimed for each file. A footer tallies the folders and files in the current location.
folders.p10: Folders are drawn as big, filled macOS-style folder icons, tinted with your theme’s accent color. zcrypt marks each one by name: a folder called Documents, Downloads, Music, Pictures, Code, or Work (and dozens of other common names) gets a matching glyph, and anything unrecognized falls back to its initial letter. A password-protected or locked folder shows a padlock instead.
folders.p11: Files sit alongside them as macOS-style tiles: image and video files show a live thumbnail, while other types show a page tile with a colored type icon and the file’s extension. You can also pick a color theme for the app in Settings (the choice is saved per device) and the interface uses soft squircle corners on browsers that support them, with clean rounded corners everywhere else.
folders.p13: Use the search box to filter the current folder by name, or the type chips to narrow to images, documents, and so on. Search runs entirely on your device against decrypted names : the server never receives your query or your file names.
folders.p15: Folder names are encrypted client-side with a key derived from your passphrase, exactly like file contents. The server only ever stores opaque ciphertext, so your folder structure is private too.
folders.p16: When your vault is locked, folders display as [locked] until you unlock. If you forget your passphrase, folder names (like file contents) cannot be recovered, because there is nothing readable on our side to recover them from.

getting-started.p1: zcrypt has no paid tiers, no credit card, and no storage to sell you. You bring your own backend: your encrypted files live in a GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account you already have, so your capacity is whatever free space those platforms give you. New accounts also get 1 GiB of shared starter space to try things before connecting anything.
getting-started.p3: Sign up at {v1} with your email and a strong account password. If email is set up on the instance, you also get a verification link; verifying it proves the address is yours.
getting-started.p4: This account password only logs you in. It is not what encrypts your files. That is the passphrase you set next, and the two are intentionally different.
getting-started.p6: On your first sign-in you create a passphrase. zcrypt uses it to derive your encryption key locally, in your browser. The passphrase and the key it derives never leave your device and are never sent to our servers. That is what makes zcrypt zero-knowledge.
getting-started.p7: Use at least 10 characters (the app enforces this for new vaults). Choose something strong and memorable, and store it in a password manager. For the full picture of how your key is derived and held, see <l1>Core concepts</l1>.
getting-started.p8: Because your passphrase never touches our servers, we cannot reset it for you. If you lose it, your files cannot be decrypted by anyone, including us. Save it somewhere safe.
getting-started.p11: zcrypt does not run a storage farm. Your encrypted data lives in a platform account you connect: GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram. Open Settings and add an access token (or a bot token and channel for Telegram). zcrypt then creates private repositories, or a private channel: on your behalf and stores your encrypted chunks there.
getting-started.p12: Want more room? Connect more than one platform. For per-platform setup and how tokens are kept, see <l1>Connect your storage</l1>.
getting-started.p14: Open your vault and drag a file onto the explorer, or click to browse. Before anything leaves your device, zcrypt does all of the following in your browser:
getting-started.p15: Splits it into chunks (4, 10, 16 or 32 MiB, tuned to your device).
getting-started.p16: Compresses each chunk with zstd, client-side, so the savings happen before encryption.
getting-started.p17: Encrypts each chunk with AES-256-GCM under a key wrapped by your passphrase, then uploads it to your connected platform.
getting-started.p18: You see real-time progress as each chunk completes. Only ciphertext ever reaches your storage platform.
getting-started.p20: Click the file to open it in the full-screen viewer, images, video, audio, PDFs, documents, and text are decrypted on the fly and rendered locally, with no plaintext leaving your device. Or download it: zcrypt fetches the chunks, reassembles, decrypts, and decompresses them back into the original file on your device.
getting-started.p21: If your vault is locked, you will be asked for your passphrase once; it then unlocks everything for the rest of your session.

glossary.p1: A few of these are general cryptography terms; the rest are specific to how zcrypt works. They build on each other, so it can help to read them in order.
glossary.p5: Your private, encrypted drive in zcrypt: the folders and files only you can decrypt. It is locked until you unlock it with your passphrase.
glossary.p7: The secret you choose to protect your vault. It is used on your device to derive your encryption keys and is never sent to or stored by the server, so it cannot be recovered if lost.
glossary.p9: The key that actually encrypts a file's contents. In an envelope scheme the CEK is itself encrypted by a higher-level key rather than used directly from your passphrase.
glossary.p11: A two-layer scheme: data is sealed with a content key (the CEK), and that content key is in turn sealed ("wrapped") by another key. It lets zcrypt re-key or re-share data without re-encrypting every byte.
glossary.p13: A piece of a file, sized to your device (4, 10, 16 or 32 MiB; 10 MiB is the usual). A file is split into chunks first, then each chunk is compressed and encrypted on its own. Chunks make uploads parallel, resumable, and easy to spread across storage repositories.
glossary.p15: Random bytes mixed into key derivation so the same passphrase produces a different key each time. zcrypt uses a unique salt per file, which defeats precomputed-hash attacks.
glossary.p17: A key whose job is to encrypt other keys rather than data. zcrypt derives a per-user KEK from the instance master key (via HKDF) to wrap your stored platform tokens at rest.
glossary.p19: An architecture where the service holds no ability to read your data, no plaintext and no keys ever cross to the server. The trade-off is that nobody, including us, can recover a lost passphrase.
glossary.p21: zcrypt's storage model: you connect your own GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account as the backend, so your encrypted data lives on infrastructure you control and your capacity is your platform's free space.
glossary.p23: The set of repositories zcrypt uses on a storage platform. As a repo nears the platform's size limit, the pool auto-rotates to a new repo, so storage grows without manual intervention.
glossary.p25: A second, innocent-looking vault opened by a separate decoy password, for plausible deniability. If compelled to log in, you can reveal the decoy instead of your real vault.
glossary.p27: An optional safeguard that notifies a trusted contact if you stop checking in within a configured window: useful for handing off access if something happens to you.
glossary.p29: Time-based One-Time Password: the six-digit, 30-second codes from an authenticator app. zcrypt uses TOTP for two-factor authentication on sign-in.
glossary.p31: Zstandard, a fast, high-ratio compression algorithm. zcrypt compresses files with zstd before encrypting them, so less data is encrypted and stored.
glossary.p33: See these terms in context: <l1>Encryption model</l1>, <l2>Zero-knowledge architecture</l2>, and <l3>Architecture</l3>.
glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.description: The vocabulary used throughout zcrypt and these docs, defined in one place.

home.p2: zcrypt is a zero-knowledge encrypted cloud drive: real folders, instant in-browser previews, and per-folder passwords, all encrypted on your device and stored in accounts you already own. These guides cover every part of it.
home.p6: The whole project is open source. Open an issue, read the code, or reach out and we'll help directly.

how-it-works.p1: When you add a file, zcrypt splits it into chunks, then compresses and encrypts each chunk, all on your device: then pushes those chunks to repositories in your own connected account. The plaintext never leaves your machine, and your passphrase never leaves your browser.
how-it-works.p5: Each chunk is compressed on your device with Zstandard (zstd). This happens before encryption, while the data is still readable and therefore still compressible: encrypted data looks random and cannot be shrunk. zcrypt skips file types that are already compressed, and keeps the compressed chunk only if it is at least 5% smaller. Smaller payloads mean less of your storage used and faster uploads.
how-it-works.p7: Each compressed chunk is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. zcrypt generates a random content encryption key (CEK) for the file, then wraps (encrypts) that CEK with a key derived from your passphrase. The wrapped CEK travels with the file's metadata; the passphrase itself never does.
how-it-works.p8: The server only ever receives ciphertext and a wrapped key it cannot open. Even if the server, the database, and your storage platform were all compromised at once, your files would stay unreadable, because the key that unwraps the CEK exists only on your device, derived from a passphrase we never see.
how-it-works.p11: The file is split into chunks sized to your device (4, 10, 16 or 32 MiB; 10 MiB is the usual). Chunking keeps each piece within platform file-size limits, enables parallel and resumable transfers, and means one failed piece can be retried without re-sending the whole file. Each chunk then goes through the next two steps on its own, and every stored chunk is given a randomized filename.
how-it-works.p12: ~10 MB is the typical size. zcrypt picks 4, 10, 16 or 32 MB based on your device, trading memory for throughput.
how-it-works.p15: Each encrypted chunk is pushed to the platform you connected. GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram: stored as an ordinary-looking binary blob under disguised filenames and commit messages. When a repository nears its size threshold, zcrypt creates a new one automatically so your vault keeps growing without you managing anything.
how-it-works.p16: The platform sees only opaque data: never your file names, never your content, never your folder structure.
how-it-works.p18: Downloading is the same pipeline run backwards, and every step still happens on your device:
how-it-works.p19: Fetch the encrypted chunks back from your repositories, several in parallel for speed.
how-it-works.p20: Verify each chunk against its SHA-256 hash, so a corrupted or tampered piece is caught before it is used.
how-it-works.p21: Decrypt the reassembled blob locally with the key unwrapped from your passphrase.
how-it-works.p22: Decompress back to the original file and save it. No plaintext ever touches the server.
