how-it-works.p26: <l1>Encryption model: the cryptographic detail behind each step</l1>
how-it-works.title: How it works
how-it-works.description: Every transformation that protects a file happens on your device, in order, before a single byte leaves it. This is the whole journey, and downloading runs it precisely in reverse.

key-management.p1: It is worth getting this distinction straight, because the two secrets do very different jobs and are handled very differently.
key-management.p9: Verified, then only a hash is stored
key-management.p16: Even if you choose to type the same value for both, they travel different paths: the passphrase is consumed locally by key derivation, while the password is checked server-side. One unlocks cryptography; the other unlocks an account session.
key-management.a17: They can be the same string, but they are not the same secret
key-management.p19: Your vault passphrase is the root of all encryption in zcrypt. It is fed through PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations with a per-file salt to derive the Key Encryption Key that wraps each file's content key. The full mechanics are in the <l1>encryption model</l1>.
key-management.p20: It is never transmitted to the server and never stored, not even hashed.
key-management.p21: It lives only in your device's memory while the vault is unlocked, and is discarded when the session ends or the vault locks.
key-management.p22: Because the server holds nothing derived from it, a strong passphrase is the single most important thing you control. New vaults require at least 10 characters; choose a long, unique one and keep it in a password manager.
key-management.p23: Recovery would require the server to hold a copy of your key, which would defeat zero-knowledge. If you lose your passphrase, your encrypted data cannot be recovered by anyone, including us. This is the deliberate cost of the guarantee.
key-management.p26: To share with another zcrypt user without ever handing a usable key to the server, every account is bootstrapped with its own X25519 keypair. It is not a third secret for you to remember: it rides on your passphrase, the same way your file keys do. The keypair is generated on your device the first time an unlocked session needs it.
key-management.p27: The public key is published to a small registry the server keeps in the clear, alongside a short fingerprint, so other members can wrap a shared key to you. It reveals nothing sensitive. That is what public keys are for.
key-management.p28: The private key never leaves your device in the clear. It is wrapped under your passphrase-derived key using the same PBKDF2 → AES-256-GCM envelope as your file keys, and only that ciphertext is stored. The server cannot unwrap it.
key-management.p29: Unlocking rehydrates it locally. When you unlock, the client fetches your wrapped private key and opens it with your passphrase in memory; if you have never published one, it generates and publishes a keypair on the spot.
key-management.p30: Because your private key is decrypted into the browser while you are unlocked, a cross-site-scripting bug becomes the threat that matters most. As defense-in-depth against it, the web app serves a strict Content-Security-Policy in production. It is enforced: the browser blocks anything the policy does not allow. (A self-hoster can downgrade it to report-only with CSP_REPORT_ONLY=1.) It is a second line of defense, not a guarantee: the web app still runs the JavaScript the site serves you, so the desktop app is the stronger option if that trust matters.
key-management.p31: Because the registry is served by us, a dishonest server could in principle hand a collaborator the wrong public key and interpose itself. Each key carries a short SHA-256 fingerprint you can compare out of band (in person, over a call) to catch exactly that. Your browser computes the fingerprint itself from the key, pins it the first time you see a collaborator’s key (trust on first use), and asks you to confirm if that key later changes. The sealing mechanics (an ephemeral-ECDH ECIES sealed-box) are in the <l1>encryption model</l1>.
key-management.a32: Fingerprints defend against a swapped key
key-management.p33: Since the private key is wrapped under your passphrase, losing the passphrase means it can no longer be unwrapped either: consistent with the rest of zero-knowledge: nothing derived from your passphrase is recoverable without it.
key-management.p36: Account passwords are hashed with bcrypt at cost factor 12 before storage. bcrypt is deliberately slow and salted per-hash, which blunts offline cracking if the database is ever exposed.
key-management.p38: At registration, your chosen password is checked against the HaveIBeenPwned database using k-anonymity: only the first five characters of its SHA-1 hash are sent, never the password itself. If it appears in known breaches, you get a warning with the count. This warns rather than blocks, and it fails open, if the breach service is unreachable, signup is not held up.
key-management.p40: You can enable time-based one-time passwords (TOTP, RFC 6238) with any standard authenticator app. Once enabled, login issues only a short-lived intermediate token until the correct code is supplied: the full session token is never minted on password alone.
key-management.p43: Sessions use signed JSON Web Tokens, with several deliberate hardening choices around them.
key-management.p44: HS256 with an explicit algorithm check. The verifier requires the header algorithm to be exactly HS256 and rejects anything else, closing the classic algorithm-confusion (e.g. alg: none) attack.
key-management.p45: Typed tokens. The short-lived token issued mid-login for the 2FA step is a distinct type and is refused at authenticated endpoints, so it can never be replayed past the second factor.
key-management.p46: Short-lived access tokens. Access tokens expire quickly and are refreshed via a longer-lived refresh token.
key-management.p47: Refresh tokens are stored hashed. Only a SHA-256 hash of each refresh token is kept, and the issuing IP address (coarsened to its /24 for IPv4 or /48 for IPv6) and user-agent are recorded, and a change of network is flagged in the logs.
key-management.p49: Every account carries a token version embedded in its access tokens. Bumping that version instantly invalidates every outstanding token for the account, a single switch to sign out all sessions everywhere, used on password change and on demand.
key-management.p50: Account recovery (forgotten password) goes through an emailed, single-use reset token: the hash of which is what we store, never the token itself.
key-management.p51: Vault recovery (forgotten passphrase) does not exist by design; see above. Account access and data access are separate problems.
key-management.p52: Refresh tokens can be revoked individually or wiped for an entire account, and all of them expire on a fixed schedule regardless.
key-management.p53: Authenticating proves who you are to the service; it does not hand the server your keys. After login you still supply your passphrase locally to decrypt: which is why even a fully compromised account session cannot read your files without it.
key-management.a54: Login does not unlock your vault

key-management.title: Passphrase & key management
key-management.description: zcrypt keeps two secrets cleanly separate: the passphrase that unlocks your encryption, and the password that authenticates your account. This page traces both, and the defenses around the sessions in between.
key-management.p62: Newer clients can also wrap your file keys under one random account master key, itself wrapped under your passphrase-derived key, so a device derives one key per unlock instead of one per file. Writing files this way is off by default and only the instance operator can turn it on; files stay readable either way. Losing the passphrase makes the master key unrecoverable too.

oauth.p1: These are two unrelated things that both mention GitHub:
oauth.p2: Signing in with GitHub (this page) uses GitHub as an identity provider to log you into your zcrypt account. It grants zcrypt nothing beyond your basic profile and email.
oauth.p3: Connecting GitHub as storage is a separate step where you add a personal access token in settings so zcrypt can store your encrypted file chunks in a repository. That is covered in Connect your storage. You can do either, both, or neither.
oauth.a4: Sign-in with GitHub ≠ GitHub as storage
oauth.p5: OAuth sign-in answers one question: who are you? Where your encrypted data lives is a completely separate decision. You could sign in with Google and store chunks on GitHub, sign in with GitHub and store on HuggingFace, or sign in with a password and store anywhere: the two choices never constrain each other.
oauth.p7: Choose Continue with Google or Continue with GitHub on the login page. zcrypt redirects you to the provider, you approve, and the provider sends you back. From there one of three things happens:
oauth.p8: Already linked, if that provider account is tied to an existing zcrypt user, you're signed straight in.
oauth.p9: Matching email, if a zcrypt account already uses the provider's email and that email is verified, the provider is auto-linked to it and you're signed in.
oauth.p10: New to zcrypt: otherwise a fresh account is created with a username derived from your name or email, and a verified email. OAuth-only accounts have no password until you add one.
oauth.p11: If a zcrypt account exists for an email that was never verified, zcrypt refuses to auto-link a provider to it and asks you to log in with your existing method first, then link in settings. This stops someone who controls a Google/GitHub account for an unverified address from quietly taking over the matching local account. Tokens are also returned to the browser in the URL fragment, so they never land in server logs or referrer headers.
oauth.p14: From your account settings you can see which providers are connected and link additional ones. Linking lets you sign in to the same zcrypt account through more than one identity: handy if you sometimes have Google handy and sometimes GitHub.
oauth.p15: You can unlink a provider just as easily, with one guardrail: zcrypt will not let you remove your last remaining sign-in method. If a provider is the only way into your account, add a password or link a second provider before unlinking it: otherwise you'd lock yourself out.
oauth.p16: Unlinking a provider only removes it as a way to sign in. It does not delete your zcrypt account, your files, or any storage backend you connected.
oauth.p18: The desktop app signs you in through your normal system browser rather than an embedded webview, so you authenticate in a trusted, full-featured browser you already use. The flow:
oauth.p19: The app starts an OAuth sign-in with a high-entropy, single-use session identifier and opens the provider in your default browser.
oauth.p20: You approve in the browser and land on a short confirmation page.
oauth.p21: The app polls a one-time endpoint for that session, receives your tokens once, and the server immediately discards them.
oauth.p22: The session identifier must carry real entropy and each result is handed out exactly once, then expires quickly, so the hand-off can't be guessed or replayed to capture your tokens. See <l1>the desktop app</l1> for the rest of the native experience.

toc.limits: What it does and doesn't do

obfuscation.p1: Encryption answers “can someone read this?” with a firm no. Obfuscation answers a different question: “does this look worth attacking?” Your encrypted chunks live in repositories on general-purpose platforms like GitHub and GitLab. If those repos were obviously a stash of encrypted secrets, they would draw attention even though the contents are unreadable. So zcrypt makes them look mundane.
obfuscation.p2: This is defense in depth. The confidentiality guarantee comes entirely from <l1>encryption</l1>; obfuscation just reduces the signal that there is anything to encrypt in the first place.
obfuscation.a3: A second layer, not a replacement
obfuscation.p5: Each encrypted chunk is stored under a random hex filename with a .bin extension: the kind of name a build tool or cache would produce. There is no sequence number, no original name, and no extension that hints at the underlying file type.
obfuscation.p8: Because names are random rather than ordered, the storage layout doesn't reveal how many files you have, how they relate, or which chunks belong together, that mapping lives only in your encrypted index.
obfuscation.p10: The repositories themselves are dressed to look like routine internal tooling rather than a storage vault:
obfuscation.p11: Plausible project names assembled from developer-flavored words: things like core-engine-v3 or shared-cache-v1.
obfuscation.p12: Rotating commit messages in conventional-commit style, such as chore: update cache artifacts or chore: refresh build cache.
obfuscation.p13: A generic README describing the repo as auto-managed build artifacts and cache storage, so a casual glance finds nothing of note.
obfuscation.p14: These repositories are created as private: the disguise is what they look like to anyone who does gain access, not an invitation for the public to browse them.
obfuscation.p17: For zcrypt to create and write these private repositories on your behalf, the storage token you connect needs the permission to do exactly that. We will be straight about it rather than calling it “minimal.”
obfuscation.p18: Connecting GitHub requires a token that can create and write to private repositories, a classic repo scope grants full control of private repos. That is the access level needed to manage your storage, not a read-only sliver.
obfuscation.p19: The same principle applies to the other backends: the token must be able to create and write the repositories or channels that hold your chunks.
obfuscation.p20: Whatever the scope, the token only ever lets zcrypt move ciphertext in and out. It confers no ability to read your files.
obfuscation.p21: Those tokens are encrypted at rest under a server-derived key, which is the one non-zero-knowledge surface in the system, detailed in <l1>zero-knowledge architecture</l1>.
obfuscation.p23: It does make storage repos blend in, strip identifying detail from filenames, and keep file relationships out of the storage layout.
obfuscation.p24: It does not hide that an account exists on the storage platform, nor the aggregate size of what is stored: a determined platform operator can see byte totals.
obfuscation.p25: It is not the thing keeping your data confidential. If obfuscation were stripped away entirely, your files would remain unreadable, because they are encrypted.
obfuscation.p26: Treat obfuscation as reducing attention, not as a confidentiality control. The security argument always rests on the encryption; the disguise is there to keep the encrypted store from standing out.
obfuscation.a27: Don't rely on it as secrecy

obfuscation.description: Strong encryption already protects your file contents. Obfuscation is the layer on top that keeps your storage from advertising itself, so the repositories holding your data read as ordinary developer projects.

organizing.p1: Drag any file or folder onto a folder to move it inside. You can also drop it onto a breadcrumb crumb to move it to that level of the tree: handy for popping an item back up several folders at once. Valid drop targets highlight as you drag.
organizing.p3: Select several items first, then drag any one of them, the whole selection moves together. Drop the group onto a folder or a breadcrumb just like a single item.
organizing.p5: Drop a file directly onto another file and zcrypt creates a new folder containing both. It is the fastest way to start grouping related files without making the folder first.
organizing.p7: Prefer a picker to dragging? Choose Move to folder on any item or selection to open a nested folder browser. Drill into the tree, pick a destination, and confirm.
organizing.p8: The picker will not let you move a folder into itself or into one of its own descendants: destinations that would create a loop are disabled, so you can't accidentally orphan a branch of your tree.
organizing.p11: The explorer supports the selection gestures you already know, plus full keyboard control:
organizing.p15: Add or remove a single item from the selection
organizing.p18: Select everything in the current folder
organizing.p23: With a selection active, you can act on all of it at once:
organizing.p24: Bulk download packages the selected files into a single ZIP. Each file is fetched, decrypted, and decompressed on your device as the archive is assembled, nothing is decrypted server-side.
organizing.p25: Bulk delete moves the whole selection to the Trash, where it can be restored or purged later.
organizing.p26: For more on archives and large multi-file jobs, see <l1>Bulk operations</l1>.
organizing.title: Moving & organizing
organizing.description: Rearrange your encrypted drive the way you would expect: drag things where they go, select in bulk, and act on many files at once: all from the unified explorer.

pad.p1: A Pad is a short-lived, encrypted note. You type or paste text, zcrypt encrypts it on your device, and you get a link to share. It’s the right tool when you need to pass along something sensitive in text form: credentials, a recovery phrase, a private message, without leaving it sitting in a chat log or email forever.
pad.p3: The text is encrypted in your browser before upload. The server receives and stores only the ciphertext. It has no way to read what you wrote. When the recipient opens the link, the ciphertext is fetched and decrypted locally in their browser.
pad.p4: Encryption and decryption happen entirely on-device.
pad.p5: The server holds opaque ciphertext and nothing more.
pad.p6: The recipient needs no account to read the note.
pad.p8: Size: up to about 1 MB of text, ample for notes, keys, and pastes, but not for files. For files, use Anonymous Send.
pad.p9: Expiry: choose 1 hour, 24 hours, or 7 days. After that the Pad expires and can no longer be opened.
pad.p11: Enable burn after read to make the Pad one-time. After the first view it is consumed and removed, so anyone who opens the link afterward sees only that it has already been read.
pad.p13: The note’s contents stay private: the server only ever stores ciphertext. For abuse prevention, the creator’s IP address is recorded alongside the Pad, coarsened to its /24 (IPv4) or /48 (IPv6) network. If that matters to you, create the Pad from a network you’re comfortable being associated with.
pad.p16: <l1>Anonymous Send: share a file instead of text</l1>
pad.p17: <l1>Sync & device transfer: push text and links to your own devices</l1>
pad.title: Encrypted Pad
pad.description: Send a snippet of text (a password, a note, a paste) that's encrypted in your browser and can be set to self-destruct after a single read. Think of it as an encrypted, expiring pastebin.

platform-adapters.p1: A storage backend (internally, a platform adapter) is the account zcrypt pushes your encrypted chunks to. By the time anything is sent, each chunk has already been compressed and encrypted with AES-256-GCM on your device, so the platform only ever sees opaque binary blobs under disguised filenames and commit messages. It never sees your file names or their contents.
platform-adapters.p2: Because it's your account, your usable space is bounded only by that platform's free space rather than by a plan we sell. zcrypt handles the encryption, chunking, and repository management on top. Until you connect an account, uploads go to zcrypt's shared storage, capped at 1 GiB per account.
platform-adapters.p4: Each file is stored on a single platform. Backends differ mostly in how much they hold per repository and how large a single piece can be: which is why zcrypt rotates across many repositories as they fill up (see <l1>Repo pool & rotation</l1>).
platform-adapters.p12: Highest API maturity; new private repos are created automatically as they fill.
platform-adapters.p16: Much larger repos than GitHub: a good middle ground for bigger vaults.
platform-adapters.p20: Free tier is 100 GB total per account (not per repo), so it fills fastest and zcrypt picks it last for automatic uploads. Supports presigned direct upload, so large files stream straight to LFS storage instead of relaying through our server.
platform-adapters.p24: The default primary backend: your chat or channel has no storage ceiling. The Bot API caps a single message at 50 MB up / 20 MB down, so zcrypt transparently splits chunks into ~19 MB parts and reassembles them on download.
platform-adapters.p25: These figures are the conservative thresholds zcrypt rotates at, chosen to stay comfortably inside each platform's real limits. On GitHub, GitLab, and Telegram your total space is not one repo: it grows across as many repositories (or, on Telegram, messages) as you need.
platform-adapters.a26: Capacities are guidance, not hard caps
platform-adapters.p27: Hugging Face's free tier is 100 GB of private storage for the whole account, so adding more repos there adds no real capacity: the per-repo threshold is kept under that account-wide ceiling on purpose. For more Hugging Face room, connect another account, or lean on Telegram, which has no ceiling at all.
platform-adapters.a28: Hugging Face is capped per account, not per repo
platform-adapters.p30: Each file lives on a single backend. When you upload without naming a platform, the default "Auto" mode: zcrypt doesn't choose at random, and it doesn't shove large files onto whichever platform looks emptiest. It follows a fixed preference order:
platform-adapters.p31: Telegram: the primary backend, because its storage is effectively unlimited.
platform-adapters.p32: GitHub, then GitLab: capable git fallbacks when no Telegram account is connected.
platform-adapters.p33: Hugging Face: deliberately last, because its free tier is a fixed 100 GB per account rather than per repo.
platform-adapters.p34: The practical upshot: a large file is kept on Telegram rather than being auto-routed onto capacity-limited Hugging Face. If you'd rather a file land somewhere specific, pick the platform explicitly at upload time. That always overrides Auto.
platform-adapters.p35: Once an upload starts, zcrypt records the chosen platform and account with the session on the server. If the transfer is interrupted and picked back up, even from another device, or after clearing your browser's storage: it resumes on that same platform from where it left off, never restarting on a different backend.
platform-adapters.a36: Resume stays on the original platform
platform-adapters.p38: You connect a backend by pasting an access token from Settings → Platform Tokens. Grant the least privilege that still lets zcrypt create repositories and read/write files:
platform-adapters.p50: Bot from @BotFather, added to a private channel/group as admin
platform-adapters.p51: For GitHub, the classic repo scope means full control of private repositories : zcrypt only ever touches the storage repos it creates, but the scope itself is broad, so use a token dedicated to zcrypt. GitLab needs api for project management plus write_repository for file operations.
platform-adapters.p52: Every platform token is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a server-side key-encryption key (KEK) before it touches the database. Even in a database breach, your tokens stay protected.
platform-adapters.p55: Telegram has no concept of repositories, so its "token" is actually two values joined with a pipe: your bot token and the target chat or channel ID.
platform-adapters.p58: Create the bot by messaging @BotFather and sending /newbot; copy the token it gives you.
platform-adapters.p59: Make a private channel or group to hold your files and add the bot to it as an administrator.
platform-adapters.p60: Use the channel's @username or its numeric ID as CHAT_ID, then paste BOT_TOKEN|CHAT_ID into zcrypt.
platform-adapters.p62: A connected token can still fail at runtime: the platform's API might be down, DNS might not resolve, or the token might have been revoked. When zcrypt can't build a working connection for a token, it doesn't silently drop the account or pretend an upload succeeded.
platform-adapters.p63: In Settings → Platform Tokens the account still shows as connected but is flagged unreachable, with a short reason such as "unreachable: connection timed out", "unreachable: DNS lookup failed", or "authentication failed (token may be revoked)".
platform-adapters.p64: A failed token isn't written off: it's only cached as unreachable briefly (about a minute) and then retried, so a transient outage clears on its own without you reconnecting.
platform-adapters.p65: The reason string is deliberately scrubbed of the underlying request details. Telegram bot tokens live inside the API URL, so echoing a raw transport error would expose them: zcrypt maps every failure to a fixed set of safe, generic reasons instead of surfacing the platform's error verbatim.
platform-adapters.a66: Error messages never leak your token
platform-adapters.a67: When a backend can't be reached
platform-adapters.p68: You can connect more than one account per platform (for example two GitHub accounts) and zcrypt keeps a separate repository pool for each. That multiplies your usable space and isolates rotation per account.
platform-adapters.p69: Administrators of a zcrypt instance can also mark a token global / managed, so users can store files without connecting any account of their own. When no personal token and no managed storage is available yet, uploads return a clear "storage not available" message instead of failing silently.

platform-adapters.description: zcrypt runs no storage farm of its own. Your encrypted chunks live inside accounts you already own (GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram) so your capacity is whatever free space those platforms give you, and the infrastructure stays under your control.

recovery.p1: “I'm locked out” can mean two completely different situations in zcrypt, and they have opposite outcomes. Knowing which one you're in tells you immediately whether recovery is possible.
recovery.p14: Getting back into your account is a normal, supported flow, because your account credentials live on the server (as hashes) where they can be reset or re-issued.
recovery.p15: Forgot your password? Request a reset link by email and choose a new one. See Authentication & 2FA.
recovery.p16: Sign in with a provider. If you linked Google or GitHub, you can log in through OAuth even without your password.
recovery.p17: Lost your authenticator? If you can still sign in another way, you can manage two-factor from settings. Keep a backup of your TOTP secret or a second sign-in method so a lost phone doesn't become a lockout.
recovery.p18: Recovering account access gets you back to your file list. It does not unlock your files: for that you still need your vault passphrase.
recovery.a19: What we can recover: account access
recovery.p20: This is the part to read twice. zcrypt is zero-knowledge: your files are encrypted on your device with keys derived from your vault passphrase, and that passphrase is never sent to the server. We hold only ciphertext.
recovery.p21: There is no reset link, no backdoor, and no support request that can recover a lost vault passphrase, not for you, and not for us. Without it, the keys that decrypt your files cannot be reconstructed, so the files (and their folder names) are permanently unreadable. This is not a limitation we can lift; it is the whole point of zero-knowledge encryption. The same protection that stops usfrom reading your data stops anyone from restoring it once the passphrase is lost.
recovery.p22: Folder passwords are the same. Any folder you secure with its own password is encrypted under a key derived from that password. Lose the folder password and that folder's contents are unrecoverable, even while the rest of your vault opens normally.
recovery.a23: If you lose your vault passphrase, your files are gone
recovery.a24: What we cannot recover: your data
recovery.p25: Because the passphrase can never be recovered, protecting it is entirely on you, and it's straightforward:
recovery.p26: Use a password manager. Store your vault passphrase (and any folder passwords) in a reputable manager like 1Password, Bitwarden, or KeePass. This is the single best thing you can do.
recovery.p27: Choose a long, memorable passphrase rather than a short complex one, length beats cleverness.
recovery.p28: Keep at least one secure offline copy somewhere only you can reach, especially before storing anything important.
recovery.p29: Never email it to yourself or paste it into a chat. That would defeat the zero-knowledge guarantee.
recovery.p30: Treat your vault passphrase like the only key to a safe deposit box you own outright. The bank can let you into the building, but if you lose the key, no one can open the box.

recovery.title: Account recovery
recovery.description: zcrypt is zero-knowledge by design, which makes recovery a two-sided story: getting back into your account is routine, but getting back the secret that decrypts your files is impossible if you lose it.

repo-pool.p1: Every backend caps how much one repository can comfortably hold: about 850 MB on GitHub, 9 GB on GitLab, 90 GiB on a Hugging Face dataset. If a vault were tied to one repo, that cap would be your ceiling. Instead, zcrypt keeps a pool of repositories per account and adds to it as needed.
repo-pool.p2: The pool is scoped to a unique combination of (you, platform, account). Connect two GitHub accounts and each gets its own independent pool; they never share or contend.
repo-pool.p4: At any moment, each pool has exactly one active repo that new chunks go to. The cycle is simple:
repo-pool.p5: zcrypt uploads chunks to the active repo.
repo-pool.p6: Before each upload it checks the active repo's tracked usage against the platform threshold.
repo-pool.p7: When the active repo reaches its threshold, zcrypt deactivates it and auto-creates a new repository to become the active one.
repo-pool.p8: New chunks flow into the new repo; the cycle repeats.
repo-pool.p9: New repositories are created private and given a plausible, developer-looking name such as fast-cache-v3 or core-worker-v7, with a description like "Internal build artifacts and cache storage." Nothing in the repo hints that it belongs to an encrypted drive. On Telegram, which has no repos, the same logic spreads files across virtual storage locations in your channel instead.
repo-pool.p10: Deactivating a full repo only stops new writes to it. Its chunks are still tracked and downloaded normally, so files you stored months ago keep working as the pool grows around them.
repo-pool.p13: Thresholds are deliberately conservative, sitting under each platform's real limits so uploads never bump into a hard wall mid-transfer.
repo-pool.p23: Virtual: spreads files across the channel
repo-pool.p24: Hugging Face's free tier is 100 GB for the entire account, not per repo, so spinning up another Hugging Face repo adds no real space. The per-repo threshold is kept under that account-wide ceiling, and when zcrypt picks a backend automatically it prefers Telegram (no ceiling) and lists Hugging Face last. To grow Hugging Face capacity, connect another account.
repo-pool.a25: Hugging Face doesn't grow by rotating
repo-pool.p27: Some platforms limit how fast you can push, not just how much you can store. GitHub, for instance, throttles sustained pushes at roughly 7 GB per hour. To avoid tripping that ceiling mid-transfer, zcrypt paces its own writes to each platform rather than hammering the API and getting rate-limited.
repo-pool.p28: Before sending each chunk, the background sync worker checks a per-platform budget over a trailing one-hour window. If pushing the chunk would exceed the limit, the worker holds it just long enough for earlier bytes to age out of the window, then sends, so short bursts go straight through and only sustained, over-cap volume is slowed.
repo-pool.p29: Only GitHub is throttled by default (~7 GB/hour); Telegram, GitLab, and Hugging Face are not rate-limited by zcrypt.
repo-pool.p30: Budgets are tracked per platform, so saturating GitHub never slows a push to GitLab or Telegram.
repo-pool.p31: The wait happens before a chunk claims a repo upload slot, so a throttled push never holds a slot idle or blocks other repos from making progress.
repo-pool.p33: zcrypt records the encrypted bytes written to each repo as uploads complete, so the "is this repo full?" check is a fast database lookup rather than a live API call on every chunk. Usage is tracked per repo, which is what lets a pool know precisely when to rotate and lets your total capacity add up across all of them.
repo-pool.p35: Chunks are staged on the server and pushed to your backend by a background worker, so a transfer doesn't depend on your browser staying open for every byte. If the server restarts, the worker re-drains any chunks still waiting and finishes pushing them.
repo-pool.p36: Resume is server-authoritative. zcrypt keys each upload to (you, the file's hash, its size), so restarting the same file: even from another device or after clearing local storage, hands back the original session instead of starting over. Chunks already pushed aren't re-sent or orphaned, and the transfer continues on the same platform it began on.
repo-pool.p38: Deleting a file (or cancelling an upload) queues its chunks for removal from the backend. A deletion worker drains that queue and calls each platform's delete API to erase the encrypted blobs; chunks that were staged but never pushed are simply removed from the server's staging area.
repo-pool.p39: Failed deletions are retried with backoff. If a chunk still can't be removed after repeated attempts it's flagged in the logs as an orphan needing manual cleanup, rather than being silently forgotten, and a startup sweep clears staging files whose database rows are gone.

repo-pool.title: Repo pool & rotation
repo-pool.description: A single repository on any platform fills up. zcrypt sidesteps that by treating your storage as a pool of repositories that grows on demand, so your usable space climbs transparently while you just keep uploading.

search.p1: Each folder has a search box that filters the current location as you type. It matches both file names and folder names, so you can narrow a busy folder to just the items you mean in a few keystrokes.
search.p3: zcrypt matches against the decrypted names held in your browser after the vault is unlocked. The matching runs entirely locally; your query is never sent anywhere. The server only ever stores encrypted names, so there is nothing for it to search even if it wanted to.
search.p4: A search term can be as revealing as a file name. Keeping the match on your device means neither your file names nor what you look for ever reach our servers.
search.p7: Alongside the search box, type-filter chips narrow the view by category: images, documents, and so on, and stack with whatever you have typed. Use them to sweep a folder down to one kind of file, then refine by name.
search.p8: Filters apply to the current folder, on top of any active search text.
search.p9: Clear the chips to return to the full listing.
search.p10: Search and filtering also appear inside the file explorer. See <l1>Folders & the file explorer</l1>.
search.title: Search & filters
search.description: Find what you need inside a folder fast, without your search ever leaving your device.

security.p1: zcrypt uses a small, deliberately boring set of well-understood primitives. There is no custom cipher and no novel construction: just standard authenticated encryption and a standard key-derivation function, run client-side via the Web Crypto API (in the browser) or native Rust (in the desktop and Android apps). The exact parameters below are shared by every client, so a file encrypted in one decrypts in any other.
security.p12: ECIES sealed-box: ephemeral ECDH, SHA-256-derived wrap key
security.p14: Per-user KEK derived from a server master key
security.p15: GCM is authenticated encryption: every ciphertext carries a 16-byte tag bound to the key and nonce. Flip a single bit of a stored chunk and decryption fails loudly rather than returning garbage. You get confidentiality and tamper-detection from one pass.
security.p17: The last row (token wrapping) is the one place zcrypt holds a key server-side, and it never touches your files. It is covered honestly in <l1>the zero-knowledge architecture</l1>.
security.p19: Your passphrase does not encrypt your files directly. Instead, every file gets its own random 256-bit Content Encryption Key (CEK). The file's chunks are encrypted with that CEK, and the CEK itself is then wrapped (encrypted) with a Key Encryption Key (KEK) derived from your passphrase. This is called envelope encryption.
security.p20: The CEK is generated fresh, at random, per file, never derived from anything you type.
security.p21: The KEK is derived from your passphrase plus the file's salt and is used only to wrap and unwrap the CEK.
security.p22: The server stores the wrapped CEK (a small base64 ciphertext) and the salt, but holds no key that can unwrap it.
security.p23: This indirection is what makes secure sharing and <l1>per-folder passwords</l1> possible without ever exposing your passphrase: zcrypt can re-wrap a file's CEK under a different key: a link's one-time share key, a folder-password key, or a key <l2>sealed to another user's public key</l2> , so a recipient (or a different password) can decrypt that one file while your master passphrase never moves. The underlying chunks are untouched; only the small wrapped CEK changes. See <l3>passphrase & key management</l3> for how keys flow end to end.
security.p24: A small number of files predate envelope encryption and were encrypted directly with the passphrase-derived key (no wrapped CEK). zcrypt detects this automatically on download, a file with no stored wrapped CEK uses the passphrase-derived key as the content key directly, so either path just works and you never have to think about it.
security.p27: The same envelope idea extends to sharing with another zcrypt account without ever handing a usable key to the server. Every account is bootstrapped with its own X25519 keypair. The public half is published to a registry the server keeps in the clear, so anyone can wrap a key to you; the private half is wrapped under your passphrase-derived key: the very same PBKDF2 → AES-256-GCM envelope used for file CEKs, so the server stores only ciphertext it cannot open.
security.p28: To grant access: for example, to a shared space and its files: the client seals the relevant symmetric key to the recipient's public key with an ECIES sealed-box: a fresh ephemeral keypair performs an X25519 Diffie–Hellman with the recipient, the shared secret is hashed with SHA-256 into an AES-256-GCM key, and the ephemeral public key is prepended so the recipient can reconstruct the secret.
security.a30: sealing a key to a recipient (conceptual)
security.p31: Only the recipient's private key can reproduce the shared secret, so only they can unseal the key. The server stores the sealed blob and the re-wrapped file envelopes and can read neither. Revoking a member is a key rotation: a new space key is generated, re-sealed to the remaining members, and every shared file's CEK re-wrapped under it, so a removed member's old grant opens nothing.
security.p32: Each published public key carries a short SHA-256 fingerprint. Compare it with your collaborator over a channel that isn't zcrypt (in person, a phone call) to rule out a substituted key: the only way an honest-but-curious server could interpose itself in the exchange. How the keypair is derived and held is covered in <l1>passphrase & key management</l1>.
security.a33: Verify a fingerprint out of band
security.p35: Keys are derived with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations against a cryptographically random 32-byte salt. The high iteration count makes each guess expensive, so brute-forcing a strong passphrase is computationally impractical. The salt is unique per file, so identical passphrases never produce identical keys and a precomputed-table attack buys an adversary nothing.
security.p38: The salt is not secret. It is stored alongside the file's metadata. The passphrase is. It is never transmitted, never written to our database, and exists only in your device's memory for the duration of an unlocked session.
security.p40: When you add a file, all of the heavy lifting happens locally: in a Web Worker in the browser, or on-device in the desktop and Android apps. The server only ever receives finished, encrypted chunks.
security.p41: Compress. Each chunk is compressed with zstd on your device, before encryption, unless that would not make it smaller. Encrypted data is effectively random and will not compress, so this order matters.
security.p42: Encrypt. Each compressed chunk is sealed with AES-256-GCM under the file's CEK, producing [12B nonce][ciphertext][16B tag].
security.p43: Hash. A SHA-256 digest is computed per encrypted chunk for integrity. The whole-file digest is a keyed HMAC-SHA256, so the server holds no plain hash of your content.
security.p44: Store. Chunks are pushed to your configured storage backend as opaque binary blobs.
security.p45: The backend does not compress anything. It merely carries a per-chunk compressed flag so the client knows whether to run zstd in reverse on the way back down. Older documentation implied server-side zstd. That was never how it worked.
security.p48: Files are split into chunks so uploads can run in parallel, resume after interruption, and stay within storage-provider size limits. The plaintext chunk size is chosen for your device: 4 MiB on constrained hardware, 10 MiB for most computers, up to 16 or 32 MiB on the strongest machines, and each encrypted chunk adds a 12-byte nonce plus a 16-byte tag of overhead. Encrypted chunks therefore top out around 32 MiB.
security.p49: Every chunk is independently authenticated by its GCM tag, so tampering with one chunk cannot silently corrupt the file.
security.p50: Per-chunk and whole-file SHA-256 digests let the client verify that what it downloaded is exactly what it uploaded.
security.p51: Because each chunk is encrypted on its own, large files stream through memory in bounded windows rather than being held whole.
security.p52: On the way back down, decryption and zstd decompression run across a device-aware pool of Web Workers, off the main thread: the same client-side pipeline as upload, just in reverse. Plaintext never leaves your device.
security.p53: A nonce and a tag are appended per chunk, not per file, so overhead is a flat ~28 bytes per chunk regardless of file size. The exact plaintext window is picked from your device's reported memory at upload time.
security.p56: Dig into the guarantees and the honest edges of this design.

security.title: Encryption model
security.description: Everything in zcrypt is encrypted on your device before it touches the network. This page documents exactly which algorithms run, in what order, and where each key lives, no hand-waving.

self-hosting.p1: A zcrypt deployment is two pieces: a stateless Go backend (the API, built into a tiny distroless container image) and a Next.js frontend. The backend talks to a PostgreSQL database and is configured entirely through environment variables. It holds no plaintext and no encryption keys (encryption and decryption happen in the browser) so the only long-lived secret you must protect is the MASTER_KEY, which wraps your connected storage tokens at rest.
self-hosting.p2: A documented template with placeholder values lives at app/backend/.env.example. Copy it to app/backend/.env and fill in your own values: the .env file is gitignored, so never commit real secrets.
self-hosting.p4: PostgreSQL: a local instance or a managed provider such as Neon. The schema is applied automatically on first boot (or run the migrate subcommand).
self-hosting.p5: Docker: the simplest way to run the backend. The repository ships a multi-stage Dockerfile at its root.
self-hosting.p6: Go 1.26+: only needed if you build the backend from source instead of using Docker.
self-hosting.p7: Node.js 20+ and Bun: for building or running the frontend.
self-hosting.p9: Build the image from the repository root, then run it with your configuration passed as environment variables. At minimum you need a database connection, a master key, a JWT secret, and your frontend origin.
self-hosting.p12: Prefer an env file? Pass --env-file app/backend/.env instead of repeating -e flags. The container listens on 8080 by default; hosts that inject a PORT variable are honoured too. To run it on a Linux server behind a Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports, no certificates to manage), follow deploy/server/README.md in the repository: it ships a Docker Compose file and a setup script.
self-hosting.p13: The MASTER_KEY is a 32-byte hex value that encrypts every stored platform token at rest. Generate a fresh one with openssl rand -hex 32 and keep it safe. If you lose it, connected storage tokens can no longer be decrypted; if it leaks, those tokens are exposed. It never encrypts your files. Those are sealed in the browser under your passphrase.
self-hosting.p16: These must be set for a production deployment. The server refuses to start without DATABASE_URL and MASTER_KEY.
self-hosting.p19: PostgreSQL connection string (e.g. a Neon serverless database). The schema migrates automatically on startup.
self-hosting.p20: 32-byte hex key (64 hex chars) for envelope encryption of platform tokens at rest. Generate with openssl rand -hex 32.
self-hosting.p21: Secret used to sign access and refresh tokens (HS256). Must be at least 32 characters. If left empty the server auto-generates an ephemeral one, so set a stable value in production or tokens stop validating after a restart.
self-hosting.p22: Public URL of your frontend. Used for email links and the post-OAuth redirect, and added to the CORS allow-list automatically. No trailing slash.
self-hosting.p23: Comma-separated list of origins allowed by CORS. Defaults to localhost if unset; FRONTEND_URL is always added on top.
self-hosting.p25: Everything below is optional. OAuth and email each switch on only when their full set of values is present.
self-hosting.p28: Public backend URL (e.g. https://api.example.com), no trailing slash. Required for OAuth: it builds the redirect_uri and must exactly match what is registered with Google/GitHub. If unset it is derived per-request, which usually breaks OAuth.
self-hosting.p29: Port to listen on (default 8080). PORT is also honoured for cloud hosts that inject it.
self-hosting.p30: Number of trusted reverse-proxy hops in front of the app. The real client IP is read that many hops in from the right of the X-Forwarded-For chain. 0 (default) ignores forwarding headers so clients cannot spoof their IP to bypass rate limits; set 1 behind a single proxy such as a Cloudflare Tunnel or a load balancer (the bundled deploy/server setup uses 1).
self-hosting.p31: Resend API key. Enables transactional email (verification, password reset, magic links). When set, RESEND_FROM is also required.
self-hosting.p33: Set to true only for local load testing, it disables all rate limiting. Never enable it in production.
self-hosting.p34: Without RESEND_API_KEY the server runs fine, but it cannot send verification or password-reset emails. If you configure email, both the API key and the from-address are validated at startup.
self-hosting.p37: Sign-in with Google or GitHub is optional. A provider is enabled only when both its client ID and secret are present.
self-hosting.p44: Register these exact redirect URIs with each provider, substituting your real BACKEND_URL:
self-hosting.p47: The backend logs the exact URIs to register at startup, and serves them (with no secrets) at GET /api/auth/oauth/config so you can verify the live configuration.
self-hosting.p49: The frontend only needs to know where the backend lives. Point it at your running backend, then run the dev server or produce a production build.
self-hosting.p54: Base URL of your zcrypt backend API. Baked in at build time, so rebuild after changing it.
self-hosting.p56: <l1>Architecture: how the pipeline, staging, sync worker, and adapters fit together</l1>
self-hosting.p57: <l1>API reference: the REST endpoints your instance exposes</l1>
self-hosting.p58: <l1>Bring your own storage: connect GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram</l1>
self-hosting.title: Self-hosting
self-hosting.description: zcrypt is open source. Run your own backend with Docker for full control over the database, master key, and storage. The frontend is a standard Next.js app you can deploy anywhere.

send.p1: Anonymous Send is the fastest way to hand off a single file when you don’t have, or don’t want to use, an account. It’s built for one-off transfers: a document to a journalist, a build to a tester, a photo to a friend. You get a link to share; the recipient needs no account either.
send.p3: The file is encrypted on your device before it leaves your browser. zcrypt then splits the ciphertext into chunks and uploads them under a disguised name so the stored object reveals nothing about the original file. You receive a token-based link to pass on; the recipient’s browser downloads the chunks, verifies them, and decrypts locally.
send.p4: The server stores only ciphertext: it cannot read the file.
send.p5: The stored chunks carry disguised filenames, not your original’s.
send.p6: No account, sign-in, or email is required to send or receive.
send.p8: Size: up to 50 MB per file. Larger files belong in your vault, where you can use a share link instead.
send.p9: Per day: anonymous senders can send up to 500 MB a day. Signing in raises the daily allowance.
send.p10: Expiry: choose a lifetime between 1 and 24 hours. When it lapses, the link reports that it has expired and the data is no longer retrievable.
send.p11: Sign in and upload the file to your vault, then create a <l1>share link</l1> : those support larger files and longer expiries.
send.p14: Turn on burn after read to make the send a one-time link. After the first successful access it is treated as already consumed, so a second visitor, or anyone who later finds the link: sees only that it has been used. Once the file has been served, the stored data is deleted, not just hidden.
send.p16: The file’s contents stay private: encryption happens in your browser and the server only ever holds ciphertext under a disguised name. For abuse prevention, the sender’s IP address is recorded with the transfer, coarsened to its /24 (IPv4) or /48 (IPv6) network. The integrity hash of the file is sealed too, so the server does not hold a plain hash of your content. If that matters to your threat model, send from a network you’re comfortable being associated with.
send.p19: <l1>Encrypted Pad: for sharing text and notes instead of files</l1>
send.p20: <l1>Share links: account-backed sharing with passwords and limits</l1>
send.title: Anonymous Send
send.description: Drop someone an encrypted file without signing up for anything. Send encrypts in your browser, stores the result under a disguised name for a short window, and can wipe it the moment it's read.

shared-vaults.p1: A shared vault, or space, is a vault you own but open up to other zcrypt users. You give it a name (and optionally a description, both sealed under the space key so the server stores them unreadable), invite members by their account email, and add files. Spaces live on their own pages (/spaces, with pages to create one, add files, and change settings), and the lists support keyboard multi-select. Every member can download the space’s files and decrypt them end-to-end, without ever learning your vault passphrase and without the server being able to read anything.
shared-vaults.p2: The trick is that a space has its own key: a random 256-bit key generated in your browser when you create the space. That key is what unlocks the space’s files, and it is handed to each member in a form only that member can open. The server stores the sealed grants and the wrapped file keys but can never combine them into anything readable.
shared-vaults.p3: The server holds only opaque ciphertext for a space: the per-member sealed space-key grants, the file keys wrapped under the space key, and members’ public keys and fingerprints. It never sees the space key, any member’s private key, file contents, or any vault passphrase, every unseal, unwrap, and decrypt happens in the browser.
shared-vaults.a4: What the server can and cannot see
shared-vaults.p6: Three layers of keys make a space work. Understanding them explains exactly why the server can host a shared vault without being able to read it.
shared-vaults.p7: Before you can join or run a space, your account needs an X25519 keypair. It’s generated in your browser the first time you unlock your vault. Your private key is wrapped under your passphrase-derived key (PBKDF2 → AES-256-GCM) before it’s stored, so the server only ever holds ciphertext for it. Your public key and a short fingerprint are stored in the clear so others can seal things to you.
shared-vaults.p9: When you create a space, your browser generates a fresh random 256-bit space key. For every member (including you) that key is sealed to their X25519 public key using an ECIES sealed box: an ephemeral X25519 keypair does ECDH with the recipient, the shared secret is hashed into an AES-256-GCM key, and the ephemeral public key rides along so the recipient can reconstruct it. Only the holder of the matching private key can open it, the server cannot, because it never has any private key.
shared-vaults.p12: An opened space key is cached in memory for the session only. It is never written to disk and is cleared on logout.
shared-vaults.p14: Each file already has its own content-encryption key (CEK). To share a file into a space, your browser unwraps that CEK with your vault passphrase, then re-wraps it under the space key and uploads only the opaque envelope. Any member downloads the file by unwrapping that envelope with the space key, no owner passphrase involved. The file’s chunks in storage never change; only a new wrapped copy of its key is added.
shared-vaults.p17: Every member holds one of three roles:
shared-vaults.p21: Download and decrypt the space’s files.
shared-vaults.p23: Download, plus add files (ones they own) and remove files from the space.
shared-vaults.p25: Everything an editor can do, plus invite and remove members, change roles, and edit the space's name and description. Only the owner can grant the admin role or change or remove another admin.
shared-vaults.p26: New members default to viewer unless you choose otherwise. Some actions are reserved for the owner regardless of anyone’s role: re-keying the space, deleting it, and granting or changing the admin role. Any member can also leave a space on their own.
shared-vaults.p27: You can only share a file you own, because sharing it means unwrapping its key with your own vault passphrase before re-wrapping it under the space key. Editors and admins can add files they own and remove any file from the space; viewers can only download.
shared-vaults.a28: Adding a file requires owning it
shared-vaults.p30: Invite by email: the account must already exist on zcrypt and have set up its encryption key (the person needs to have signed in and unlocked their vault at least once). If they haven’t, the invite is rejected until they do, because there’s no public key to seal the space key to.
shared-vaults.p31: Pick a role when inviting: viewer, editor, or admin (only the owner can invite someone as admin). Re-inviting an existing member updates their role and re-issues their key grant.
shared-vaults.p32: Remove a member at any time as the owner or an admin (only the owner can remove an admin). Removal flags the space for a re-key; see below.
shared-vaults.p33: Delete the space as the owner. The underlying files stay in each owner’s vault; only the sharing is torn down.
shared-vaults.p34: Each member is shown with the fingerprint of their public key, the first 16 hex characters of its SHA-256, grouped like A1B2-C3D4-E5F6-7890. Your browser computes each fingerprint itself from the member’s key, pins it the first time you see it (trust on first use), and asks you to confirm if the key ever changes. Compare that against the fingerprint the member sees in their own encryption-key settings, over a channel the server doesn’t control (in person, a call, a signed message). Matching fingerprints rule out a server that tried to swap in its own key to eavesdrop. If a member hasn’t published a key yet, no fingerprint is shown and you can’t grant them access.
shared-vaults.p37: Add files (owner, editor, admin). Pick files or whole folders from your vault. Each one’s key is re-wrapped under the space key in your browser; the server stores only the re-wrapped envelope. Files are added in the background with a progress strip, in batches. On the free plan one add carries at most 200 files by default (the instance operator can change the cap).
shared-vaults.p38: Download (any member): the space key unwraps the file’s envelope and the chunks are decrypted locally. Access is authorised through your membership without ever loosening the owner’s file scoping; an unauthorised request is indistinguishable from a plain not-found.
shared-vaults.p39: Remove files (editor, admin): unshares the file from the space. The original file is untouched in the owner’s vault.
shared-vaults.p40: A space can carry an optional size limit, set when you create it. It caps the total original size of the files shared into the space and is enforced on the server when a file is added: adds that would exceed the cap are rejected. Re-adds during a re-key don’t count twice, so rotation never trips the limit. Leave it blank for no limit.
shared-vaults.p42: Removing a member has to be more than deleting a database row, that member may have already opened the space key in their browser. So removal triggers a re-key: your browser generates a brand-new space key, seals it to every remaining member, and re-wraps every shared file’s key under the new key. The removed member gets no new grant, and because every file now answers to a new key, any copy of the old key they kept is useless going forward. This is what makes removal a true revocation, not just a hidden button.
shared-vaults.p43: Automatic on removal: when the owner removes someone, the re-key runs right after. If it doesn’t complete (for example, the space wasn’t unlocked), you’re told to finish it with the manual Re-key. When an admin removes someone, the space is flagged as needing a re-key and adding files pauses until the owner runs it.
shared-vaults.p44: Manual Re-key: the owner can rotate the space key at any time from the members panel, to rotate periodically or to complete an interrupted revocation.
shared-vaults.p45: Owner-gated: only the owner can re-key. A re-key hands out fresh grants to everyone, so it’s deliberately kept out of non-owner hands.
shared-vaults.p46: A re-key is applied atomically and must supply a fresh grant for every current member. The server rejects a partial rotation, so files can never be moved onto a new key while a member is left stranded on the old one. Re-keying needs the space to be unlocked, since your browser uses the old key to re-wrap the files under the new one.
shared-vaults.p48: Rotating the key stops a removed member from opening the space’s files from that point on. Like any sharing system, it can’t recall data they already downloaded: plaintext that has left the space is beyond its reach.
shared-vaults.p51: End-to-end sharing works today: sealed per-member key grants, file-key re-wrapping, fingerprint verification, and revocation-by-rotation all ship. It’s marked beta because the workflows and surfaces around it are still evolving. Every member needs their encryption keypair set up before they can be granted access, and sharing or re-keying requires the relevant vault or space to be unlocked in your session.
shared-vaults.p54: <l1>Passphrase & key management: your encryption keypair and fingerprint</l1>
shared-vaults.p55: <l1>Share links: share a single file end-to-end without an account</l1>
shared-vaults.p56: <l1>Zero-knowledge: the model these guarantees rest on</l1>
shared-vaults.title: Shared vaults
shared-vaults.description: Shared vaults (spaces) let a group work on the same set of end-to-end encrypted files. Each space carries its own key, sealed to every member so only members can open its files, and the server only ever holds ciphertext it cannot read.

toc.key-in-fragment: The key lives in the link

sharing.p1: From any file in your vault, choose Share to mint a public link. zcrypt generates a random share token for the URL and wraps the file’s content-encryption key under a fresh share key so the recipient can decrypt without ever knowing your passphrase.
sharing.p2: The resulting link has two parts that do very different jobs:
sharing.p4: Need to hand over more than one file? See <l1>Share a folder</l1> for a single public link that covers a whole folder, the same zero-knowledge way.
sharing.p6: Everything after the # is the URL fragment. Browsers never transmit the fragment to the server: it stays in the address bar and is only readable by JavaScript running on the page. zcrypt puts the share’s decryption key there, so our servers store only the token, the encrypted file, and a wrapped key they can never unwrap.
sharing.p7: Anyone with the full link can open the file, because the link itself carries the key. Treat a share link like the file’s password: send it over a channel you trust, and add a separate password (below) when the link might travel over something you don’t.
sharing.a9: The key lives in the link, not on our servers
sharing.p10: Each link can carry its own guardrails, all optional and all enforced on our side independently of the key in the fragment:
sharing.p14: A second secret the recipient must enter. It is hashed with bcrypt on the server and checked before any file metadata or chunks are released. Until the right password is provided, the link won’t even reveal the file name or size.
sharing.p16: Choose 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or never. After it lapses the link reports that it is no longer available.
sharing.p18: Cap the number of accesses. Once the count reaches the limit, the link stops working.
sharing.p20: Recipients need no zcrypt account. Opening the link loads a public page that fetches the encrypted chunks, verifies them, and decrypts the file entirely in their browser using the key from the fragment. The plaintext is reassembled on their device and never on our servers.
sharing.p21: If you set a password, the page prompts for it first.
sharing.p22: If the link has expired or hit its download limit, the page explains that it is no longer available.
sharing.p24: You can revoke any share link at any time from your list of shares. Revocation is immediate: the server refuses all further requests for that token, so even someone holding the full link (key and all) can no longer fetch the file.
sharing.p26: The download counter increments when a recipient’s browser fetches the link’s file metadata: the step that precedes the actual chunk downloads. It is a close proxy for “times opened,” not a byte-exact count of completed downloads, so a page reload or an interrupted download can move the number. Keep that in mind if you set a tight download limit.
sharing.p29: Other ways to get data to people and devices:
sharing.p30: <l1>Share a folder: one public link for a whole folder</l1>
sharing.p31: <l1>Anonymous Send: send a file with no account at all</l1>
sharing.p32: <l1>Encrypted Pad: share a one-time encrypted note</l1>
sharing.p33: <l1>Sync & device transfer: move data between your own devices</l1>
sharing.title: Share links
sharing.description: Hand a single file to someone with a link. zcrypt puts the decryption key in the part of the URL that never reaches our servers, so the share stays zero-knowledge, and you stay in control with optional passwords, expiry, limits, and instant revocation.

snapshots-integrity.p1: Snapshots live under the Inventory tab in Tools. A snapshot captures a point-in-time manifest of your current file list, a labelled record of what files existed in your vault when you took it. You can create snapshots, label them, list them, and delete them, giving you a timeline of how your vault’s contents have grown or changed.
snapshots-integrity.p3: A snapshot is a record of the list, not a backup of the files themselves. There is no rollback or version history yet, you cannot restore a deleted file or revert a file to a previous version from a snapshot. Use snapshots to see what your vault looked like, not to recover it. If you need to undo a deletion, check the Trash before it’s purged.
snapshots-integrity.p6: The integrity monitor (the Verify Files tab in Tools) records each file’s SHA-256 hash and size as a reference point, then compares the current file against that reference to flag anything whose hash has changed. Because the hash is computed over the file’s exact bytes, even a single altered byte changes it.
snapshots-integrity.p7: Take a reference: record a file’s hash and size as its known-good baseline.
snapshots-integrity.p8: Check: compare a file against its latest reference to see if it still matches.
snapshots-integrity.p9: Review changes: list the files whose hash no longer matches their reference.
snapshots-integrity.p11: Snapshots and the integrity monitor are still maturing. They’re useful for keeping tabs on your vault, but expect the workflows and surfaces around them to keep evolving, and don’t treat them as a substitute for a proper backup or a finished version-control system.
snapshots-integrity.p14: <l1>Timed vaults: group files under a countdown label (Timed Vaults tab)</l1>
snapshots-integrity.p15: <l1>Downloading: how files are fetched, verified, and decrypted</l1>
snapshots-integrity.p16: <l1>Shared vaults: collaborative vaults with role-based access</l1>
snapshots-integrity.title: Snapshots & integrity
snapshots-integrity.description: Lightweight tools for keeping an eye on the shape of your vault: a snapshot records what was in it at a moment in time, and the integrity monitor watches for files whose contents change unexpectedly.

sync-transfer.p1: Offline pins let you mark specific files to keep available on a given device. Pinning is per device: each browser is given its own random device id (kept locally on that device), and your pins are recorded against that device, so every device keeps its own list, and pinning or unpinning on one doesn’t change the others.
sync-transfer.p2: Pick a device: the tab shows the current device’s short id, so you can tell which device you’re pinning for.
sync-transfer.p3: Pin or unpin: toggle any file in your vault to add or remove it from that device’s offline list.
sync-transfer.p4: Stays private: a pin only records which file you want kept on hand, the file itself stays encrypted, exactly as it is in your vault.
sync-transfer.p6: Clipboard sync keeps a short, shared history of small snippets available across the sessions where you’re signed in. Add a snippet on one device and it appears on the others in real time, ready to copy.
sync-transfer.p7: Item types: text and links. A snippet that is a lone http(s) URL is tagged as a link; everything else is text. The web tool captures typed or pasted text only, there is no image capture.
sync-transfer.p9: Retention: each snippet is deleted automatically 24 hours after you add it, and only your most recent snippets are kept (the server retains the latest 30).
sync-transfer.p11: Each snippet is encrypted in your browser with a 256-bit AES-GCM key before it’s sent. That key is generated on your device and stored only in the browser, it never leaves the device and is never sent to the server. When you add a snippet, the server stores only the ciphertext plus lightweight metadata (its id, type, size, and timestamp) and pushes a live SSE (server-sent events) “clipboard” event to your other signed-in sessions so they can pull it. Fetching a snippet returns the ciphertext, which is decrypted locally.
sync-transfer.p12: The server only ever holds the snippet as ciphertext and the metadata it needs to wake up your other sessions. It never receives the encryption key and cannot read a snippet’s contents.
sync-transfer.p14: Because the key lives only in the browser and isn’t synced by the server, a device has to hold the matching key to read a snippet. A device without it will show a “different device key” notice instead of the plaintext, the trade-off of keeping the key entirely on your side.
sync-transfer.a15: Each device needs the same key
sync-transfer.p17: Folder sync lets you register local folder paths that the zcrypt desktop client should back up automatically. The web app is only for configuration: you add a folder path and an optional label, and toggle each one active or paused. The browser never reads or uploads the files in those folders, that work is done by the desktop client.
sync-transfer.p18: The backup runs while the desktop app is open on the device where those folders live.
sync-transfer.p19: Deleting a folder configuration only stops future syncing for it. Files that were already backed up stay in your vault.
sync-transfer.p22: The separate Transfer tab streams a file from one device to another in real time through a relay that stores nothing. The sending device gets a 6-digit room code and a separate pairing key. Scan the QR code (or open the link), or type both on the receiving device, and the file flows while both stay connected.
sync-transfer.p23: Encrypted before it leaves: the file and its name are encrypted in your browser and sent in small chunks over a WebSocket relay. The key is derived from the pairing key, which travels only in the QR code, link fragment or what you type, never through the relay.
sync-transfer.p24: Confirmation code: both screens show the same short code once paired. If they differ, stop and start a new room.
sync-transfer.p25: Nothing stored: the relay keeps the pairing room only in memory, and it can still see that a transfer happened and roughly how large it is; the room is torn down as soon as the transfer finishes, and an unclaimed room expires after about 10 minutes.
sync-transfer.p26: Both online at once: because the file streams straight between the two devices, both must be connected at the same time. If the connection drops mid-transfer, just start a new room.
sync-transfer.p27: Device-to-device transfer needs both ends connected together. If you need someone to pick a file up later, use <l1>Anonymous Send</l1> or a <l2>share link</l2> instead, both store the encrypted file so the recipient can fetch it on their own schedule.
sync-transfer.p31: <l1>Share links: password, expiry, and download limits</l1>
sync-transfer.p32: <l1>Encrypted Pad: share a one-time encrypted note</l1>
sync-transfer.title: Sync & device transfer
sync-transfer.description: Keep your own devices in step without handing anyone your plaintext. The Sync & Offline tab holds three tools (offline pins, encrypted clipboard sync, and folder sync) while a separate Transfer tab streams a file straight from one device to another.

tech-stack.p1: zcrypt is one product across three surfaces: web, desktop, and Android, sharing a single design principle: all encryption happens on your device, and the server only ever handles ciphertext. That principle drives the stack. The backend stays deliberately thin (standard-library Go, no framework), the cryptography lives in code that runs on the client (a Rust core for native, Web Workers for the browser), and the database stores only metadata and encrypted blobs.
tech-stack.p2: Exact versions live in app/backend/go.mod, app/frontend/package.json, and app/core/Cargo.toml. The numbers below reflect the current tree and may drift slightly ahead of a release.
tech-stack.p5: A stateless HTTP service written in Go with the standard library only, no web framework, just net/http. It brokers the chunked upload/download API, coordinates the storage adapters, and holds no plaintext and no encryption keys.
tech-stack.p11: Fast, statically linked, tiny distroless container.
tech-stack.p14: No framework: fewer moving parts, easy to audit.
tech-stack.p17: Raw SQL against PostgreSQL, no ORM.
tech-stack.p23: Server-side crypto only wraps platform tokens and re-seals metadata during key rotation; file crypto and compression are client-side.
tech-stack.p25: The browser client is a Next.js App Router application. The full encryption pipeline runs here in a pool of Web Workers, so compression, encryption, and hashing happen off the main thread: the server never sees a plaintext byte.
tech-stack.p43: Desktop and Android run zcrypt-core, a shared Rust crate that implements the same zero-knowledge crypto and chunk pipeline as the web workers, compiled to native code and embedded in-process, so there is no subprocess. The native shell is Tauri v2.
tech-stack.p49: Crypto, chunk pipeline, local ledger, platform adapters.
tech-stack.p55: Native window + OS integration on macOS, Windows, Linux, Android.
tech-stack.p58: Offline resume, dedup lookups, sync cursor.
tech-stack.p59: See <l1>Desktop app</l1> and <l2>Android app</l2> for how the shared core reaches each platform.
tech-stack.p61: The cryptographic format is identical across every surface and pinned by conformance vectors, so a file encrypted in one client decrypts in any other.
tech-stack.p72: zstd (per-chunk, skipped when it wouldn't help)
tech-stack.p74: X25519 ECIES key-wrapping (keys move, never plaintext)
tech-stack.p76: A PostgreSQL database is the index that ties everything together, users, folders, per-file salts, chunk references, encrypted platform tokens, and shares. It holds no readable file contents and no passphrase. Your actual encrypted bytes never live on zcrypt's infrastructure at all: they go to a storage platform you own.
tech-stack.p82: Raw SQL via pgx / pgxpool, no ORM
tech-stack.p84: GitHub · GitLab · Hugging Face · Telegram (bring your own)
tech-stack.p86: Deployment is intentionally boring and portable. The backend is a small distroless Docker image that runs on any Linux host; nothing about it is tied to a specific provider, which is the point. You can self-host the exact same image (see <l1>Self-hosting</l1>).
tech-stack.p92: Distroless Docker image on a cloud Linux VM (provider-agnostic)
tech-stack.p96: Your own GitHub / GitLab / Hugging Face / Telegram accounts
tech-stack.p97: Because encryption is client-side, our hosting only ever handles ciphertext and metadata. Compromising the frontend, the backend VM, or the database would not expose your files: the keys to decrypt them exist only on your devices.
tech-stack.a98: What our infrastructure can and can't see
tech-stack.p100: For how these pieces move data at runtime, read <l1>Architecture</l1>. To run the whole stack yourself, see <l2>Self-hosting</l2>, and to build on it, <l3>Contributing</l3>.
tech-stack.title: Tech stack & infrastructure
tech-stack.description: Everything zcrypt is built with, layer by layer, and how each piece is deployed. Versions track the repository; the manifests (go.mod, package.json, Cargo.toml) are the source of truth.

toc.not-protected: What it does not protect against

threat-model.p1: The architecture is built so that the most likely and most damaging server-side compromises yield nothing usable.
threat-model.p2: Server or database breach. An attacker with our full database gets ciphertext, wrapped keys they cannot unwrap, and bcrypt hashes. File contents stay sealed.
threat-model.p3: Storage-provider access. Your chunks live on GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram: all of which see only encrypted .bin blobs, never plaintext.
threat-model.p4: Man-in-the-middle. Transport is TLS, and the payload is already encrypted client-side, so intercepting traffic reveals ciphertext on top of ciphertext.
threat-model.p5: Insider access. No one operating zcrypt can read your files. There is no internal tool, key escrow, or admin override that decrypts user data, the keys simply are not on our side.
threat-model.p6: Metadata leakage. Folder names are encrypted client-side, and stored chunks are disguised with random filenames, plausible repository names, and generic commit messages. See storage obfuscation.
threat-model.p8: No client-side encryption scheme can defend everything. These are the real gaps, stated plainly.
threat-model.p9: A compromised device. Encryption happens on your machine, so malware or a keylogger that already has your device can capture your passphrase as you type it or read decrypted data from memory. Endpoint security is on you.
threat-model.p10: Metadata the server can see. Names are sealed, but the server still knows file sizes, timestamps, and the sharing graph (who shared what with whom). IPs in sessions and logs are coarsened to a /24 (IPv4) or /48 (IPv6) network, but a network-level view remains.
threat-model.p11: A weak passphrase. 600,000 PBKDF2 iterations slow guessing down dramatically, but they cannot save a passphrase that is short or common. If it can be guessed, the derived key can be reproduced.
threat-model.p12: Frontend supply-chain risk. The web app is code we serve, so in principle a compromised build could be made to exfil a passphrase. This is mitigated by the project being open source (you can audit and self-host it) and by an enforced Content-Security-Policy, but you still trust the JavaScript the site serves. The desktop app does not load code from the site and is the stronger option.
threat-model.p13: zcrypt removes us and the storage providers from your trust boundary. It cannot remove your device or the strength of your passphrase from it: those remain yours to protect.
threat-model.a15: What it does not protect against
threat-model.p21: Only ciphertext and unusable wrapped keys are stored
threat-model.p30: No keys exist on the server to misuse
threat-model.p39: Older files may keep a plaintext name until the web app re-seals it
threat-model.p42: Tokens are encrypted at rest under a server master key
threat-model.p45: Plaintext and passphrase are exposed on-device
threat-model.p48: A guessable passphrase reproduces the key
threat-model.p51: Mitigated by open source and self-hosting
threat-model.p52: The two “partial” rows on file names and storage tokens are explained in full in <l1>zero-knowledge architecture</l1> . We would rather flag them here than quietly mark everything green.
threat-model.p54: Use a long, unique passphrase from a password manager. This is the highest-leverage thing you can do.
threat-model.p55: Enable TOTP two-factor authentication on your account, covered in key management.
threat-model.p56: Keep the device you use with zcrypt patched and free of untrusted software.
threat-model.p57: For the strongest assurance, audit the open-source code or use the desktop app, which avoids browser-delivered JavaScript.
threat-model.p58: Put sensitivity-by-name files inside an <l1>encrypted folder</l1> rather than relying on the file name being hidden.
