threat-model.description: A security tool is only as honest as its threat model. Here is what zcrypt is designed to stop, what it cannot, and why, so you can decide whether it fits your situation rather than taking a slogan on faith.

timed-vaults.p1: Timed vaults live under the Timed Vaults tab in Tools. A timed vault is a lightweight label over files you have already uploaded. It has a name, an optional description, a countdown, and the list of files it groups. It is an organisational layer, not a new place to store data: creating one does not move, copy, or re-encrypt anything. Your files remain individually encrypted exactly as they were before, and each one still appears in your normal vault.
timed-vaults.p3: Open the Timed Vaults tab, choose Create vault, and fill in:
timed-vaults.p4: Name (required): how the vault shows up in the list, e.g. “Tax Documents 2026”.
timed-vaults.p5: Description (optional): a short note for your own reference.
timed-vaults.p6: Expires in. Pick a window: 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or 90 days. The countdown starts from the moment you create the vault.
timed-vaults.p7: Files: tick one or more files from your existing vault to include. You group files that are already uploaded; a timed vault is not an upload flow.
timed-vaults.p8: The shortest window is one hour: the server rejects any expiry that is less than an hour away.
timed-vaults.p10: Each vault shows a live countdown of the time remaining (for example 3d 5h). A periodic sweep on the server checks for vaults whose time has run out and marks them as expired; this runs on a schedule rather than to the exact second, so a just-lapsed vault flips over shortly after its deadline. Once flagged, the vault is dimmed in the list and carries an Expired badge instead of a countdown.
timed-vaults.p12: Expiry is a status flag, not a self-destruct. When a timed vault expires, the vault is marked expired and dimmed, but the files inside it are not deleted, moved, or altered. There is no automatic destruction: every file stays in your vault, fully intact, and remains available exactly as before. Do not rely on a timed vault to make sensitive files disappear on their own.
timed-vaults.a13: Timed vaults do not delete anything
timed-vaults.p15: Removing a timed vault deletes the vault and its timer only, the grouping and the countdown go away, but the files it referenced are left untouched in your vault. If you actually want to remove the underlying files, delete them from your file list the usual way; that is a separate action.
timed-vaults.p17: Timed vaults are still maturing. Today they are best understood as a way to label and track a set of files against a deadline, not as a retention or auto-deletion policy. Treat the countdown as a reminder, and expect the workflow around it to keep evolving.

timed-vaults.p21: <l1>Shared vaults: collaborative vaults with role-based access</l1>

timed-vaults.description: Group files you have already uploaded under a single named countdown. When the timer lapses the vault is flagged as expired and dimmed in the list, but nothing self-destructs, and your files stay exactly where they are.

toc.not-device: Not the same as device transfer

transfer-manager.p1: The transfer manager is a docked panel in the bottom-right of the app. It is mounted once for the whole authenticated app, so it survives navigation: start an upload, open another folder, preview a file: your transfers keep going and stay visible. When there's nothing in flight and nothing finished to review, the panel simply isn't there.
transfer-manager.p2: It also stays out of your way without hiding work: the dock stays visible while anything is active or has failed, and can't be swiped away while a transfer is in flight: only a fully-settled dock can be flicked aside, and it comes back the moment a new transfer starts. If you try to close the tab while transfers are actively moving, the browser warns you first, since closing would kill the chunks in flight.
transfer-manager.p3: Uploads and downloads share the panel. In-flight work sorts to the top and finished work sinks to the bottom, with a header summarizing how many transfers are active or failed and a Clear completed action to tidy up.
transfer-manager.p5: Each transfer shows its own live status, and what you can do depends on its direction and state:
transfer-manager.p6: Direction at a glance: an animated arrow marks every row: an upload arrow nudging up, a download arrow nudging down, so you can tell which way a transfer is going without reading the label.
transfer-manager.p7: Progress, speed & ETA: a per-item progress bar whose fill tracks the true byte ratio (so it never appears to stall), with an estimated time remaining. Uploads add a live transfer speed drawn from a smoothed byte rate.
transfer-manager.p8: Pause / Resume: for uploads and downloads: hold a transfer without losing what's already done, then continue where it left off.
transfer-manager.p9: Retry, re-run a failed transfer. A single file continues from what's already done rather than starting over; a multi-file ZIP restarts.
transfer-manager.p10: Stop / Cancel: end a download (Stop) or an upload (Cancel) that's in progress. This is the destructive action, distinct from Pause.
transfer-manager.p11: Dismiss: clear a finished or interrupted row from the list. For an unfinished upload this is non-destructive (below).
transfer-manager.p13: Pausing an upload stops it at a chunk boundary: it finishes the chunk in flight and then holds, so the server-side upload session and the per-file key are preserved. Resuming continues from the chunks already uploaded rather than starting over, re-using that same session and key. Downloads pause the same way: a paused download keeps everything decrypted so far (and, for a large download streaming to disk, the open file), and resumes from there. Pausing is deliberately distinct from Stop / Cancel, a pause preserves state, a stop discards it.
transfer-manager.p14: The two directions differ in how long a hold survives. An interrupted upload's progress is tracked on the server, so you can pick it back up even after a reload or closing the tab. A download's partial state lives only on your device, so closing the tab restarts it. See <l1>Downloading</l1>.
transfer-manager.p15: Resume and retry need your key locally to encrypt or decrypt the remaining chunks, but the manager never prompts for it and never forwards it anywhere, it reads the passphrase already cached for your unlocked vault. For a transfer into a <l1>protected folder</l1>, resume uses that folder's password, so the folder must be unlocked first; otherwise the manager asks you to open it rather than risk encrypting chunks with the wrong key.
transfer-manager.a16: The panel never asks for your passphrase
transfer-manager.p18: There are two ways to clear a row, and they mean different things. Dismiss: the ✕ on a finished row, or a sideways swipe on a settled dock : just removes the row from the panel. For an upload that hasn't finished, dismiss is non-destructive: it hides the row but leaves the upload's server-side session intact, so a stray swipe can never delete a partial upload. Downloads have no server-side state, so dismissing one just removes its row. Cancel (uploads) and Stop (downloads) are the destructive actions that actually end a transfer.
transfer-manager.p19: Because an unfinished upload's session lives on the server, you have a week to resume it (after a pause, a failure, or even closing the tab) before it's cleaned up. Unfinished uploads show up as resumable rather than being lost.
transfer-manager.a20: Interrupted uploads are kept for 7 days
transfer-manager.p22: When you want it out of the way, collapse the panel down to a compact pill that shows a single aggregate progress bar across all running transfers. Expand it again any time to see the full per-item list.
transfer-manager.p24: The transfer manager described here tracks ordinary uploads and downloads between your device and your storage. It is not the peer-to-peer device transfer tool, which moves a file directly between two of your devices. Device transfer is covered separately in Sync & device transfer.

transfer-manager.title: Transfer manager
transfer-manager.description: A single docked panel, pinned to the corner of the app, that gathers every upload and download in one place, and keeps running, and stays visible, as you move around your drive.

trash.p1: Deleting a file moves it to Trash rather than removing it outright, a soft delete. The file leaves your folders but its encrypted chunks stay on your storage platform, untouched, so it can be brought back.
trash.p3: From Trash, restore an item to return it to your vault. Because nothing was actually purged, a restore is instant and complete: the file comes back exactly as it was.
trash.p5: To reclaim space, choose delete forever. This is the irreversible step: zcrypt purges the file's chunks from every connected storage platform they live on. After a purge there is nothing left to restore.
trash.p6: Delete-forever cannot be undone. Once the chunks are purged from your platforms, the file is gone for good: restore anything you might still want before you purge.
trash.p9: Not sure whether to keep something? You can preview items in Trash with the same full-screen viewer used elsewhere, so you can confirm exactly what a file is before restoring or purging it. See Viewing & previewing files.
trash.p11: Trash supports bulk selection, so you can clear out or recover many items in one pass:
trash.p12: Select multiple items, then restore the whole group at once.
trash.p13: Or delete the selection forever to purge several files' chunks together.
trash.title: Trash & restore
trash.description: Deletes are reversible by default. Items go to Trash first, so a mis-click is a quick restore, until you decide to purge them for good.

troubleshooting.p1: If decryption keeps failing or you land in a unlock/Retry loop, the most likely cause is a passphrase that doesn't match the one a file was encrypted with, a typo, a different keyboard layout, or an old passphrase. zcrypt can't tell you the passphrase is wrong before it tries to decrypt, because there's nothing readable on the server to check it against.
troubleshooting.p2: Re-enter the passphrase carefully: watch for caps lock and trailing spaces.
troubleshooting.p3: Lock the vault and unlock again to clear any cached attempt, then retry.
troubleshooting.p4: If you have multiple accounts, confirm you're signed into the right one.
troubleshooting.p5: A passphrase is never stored and cannot be reset. If it's truly gone, the affected files cannot be recovered. See <l1>Account recovery</l1>.
troubleshooting.p8: A password-protected folder is sealed under its own key, separate from your account passphrase. Having the vault unlocked is not enough: the folder stays locked until you enter its specific password.
troubleshooting.p9: Open the folder and enter the folder password (not your account passphrase) when prompted.
troubleshooting.p10: Remember that each protected folder can have a different password. Use the one set for that folder.
troubleshooting.p11: If you removed the password earlier, the folder's files were re-keyed back to your account passphrase; unlock the vault normally.
troubleshooting.p14: Uploads are chunked and resumable, so a stall is rarely fatal. If progress stops, a dropped connection, a closed tab, a sleeping laptop: the chunks already received are kept server-side, and the transfer can pick up where it left off.
troubleshooting.p15: Retry or resume the transfer from the transfer manager: only the missing chunks are re-sent.
troubleshooting.p16: Check your network connection; large files over flaky links may pause and resume several times.
troubleshooting.p17: Leave the tab open while a big upload finishes, or use the desktop app for long transfers.
troubleshooting.p18: See <l1>Transfer manager</l1> for pause, resume, and retry controls.
troubleshooting.p20: Each storage platform has its own size ceiling per repository, and zcrypt stores a given file's chunks on a single platform. A single file can be at most 10 GiB, and a very large file can exceed what a platform comfortably holds. zcrypt rotates to a fresh repository automatically as repos fill, but the headroom still varies a lot between backends.
troubleshooting.p21: For large files, use Telegram: it has no storage ceiling and is what Auto picks first. Hugging Face is capped at 100 GB per free account, so it does not add room by itself.
troubleshooting.p22: Confirm the target platform actually has free space; rotation creates new repos but can't exceed your account's quota.
troubleshooting.p23: Splitting a huge archive into smaller files can also help spread it across the pool.
troubleshooting.a25: File too large for a platform
troubleshooting.p26: If uploads or downloads start failing for a whole platform, its access token may have been revoked, expired, or had its scopes changed on the provider's side. zcrypt can't push or pull chunks without a valid token.
troubleshooting.p27: Open Settings and check the platform's connection status.
troubleshooting.p28: Reconnect the platform with a fresh token that has the required scopes.
troubleshooting.p29: If you rotated the token on the provider (GitHub, GitLab, and so on), update it in zcrypt to match.
troubleshooting.p30: Token setup is covered in <l1>Bring your own storage</l1>.
troubleshooting.p32: The API limits how many requests an IP can make in a short window to keep the service healthy and to blunt brute-force attempts. Auth and public share/send links are limited more tightly. A burst of activity (or retrying too aggressively after a failure) can trip these limits.
troubleshooting.p33: Wait a short while, then retry: limits reset on a rolling window.
troubleshooting.p34: Avoid hammering retries in a tight loop; space them out.
troubleshooting.p35: On your own self-hosted instance behind a proxy, make sure the trusted-proxy setting is correct so legitimate traffic isn't grouped under one IP.
troubleshooting.p36: Some failures originate with the storage provider, not zcrypt. If a single platform is throttling you, give it time and the sync worker will retry the affected chunks.
troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.description: The handful of issues people hit most, and how to clear them. Most have a simple cause: the wrong key, a transient network hiccup, or a platform limit doing its job.

uploading.p1: By the time an upload begins, the file is split into chunks on your device, and each chunk has been compressed with zstd and encrypted with AES-256-GCM (see <l1>How it works</l1>). What gets sent is a sequence of encrypted chunks: the server receives only ciphertext.
uploading.p2: Chunks are sized to your device: 4, 10, 16 or 32 MiB, from a memory-constrained phone up to a powerful desktop, with 10 MiB the common middle. The chosen size is recorded server-side, so a resume from any device re-slices the file at exactly the same boundaries: a mismatched size would misalign every chunk after the first.
uploading.p3: An upload starts by opening a session that records the file’s metadata, salt, wrapped key, chunk count, and chunk size. Each chunk is then sent with its own SHA-256 hash, which the server checks on arrival; a chunk whose bytes don’t match its hash is rejected.
uploading.p5: Uploads are resumable, and the design makes resuming reliable rather than best-effort:
uploading.p6: Incoming chunks are staged durably on the server and recorded in the database before the platform push, so they survive a server restart.
uploading.p7: A status endpoint reports which chunk indices have already been received: including chunks still staged and merely waiting on the background push. Resume counts those too, so it never re-sends bytes the server already holds.
uploading.p8: On resume, the client asks for that status and continues from the chunks still missing, re-using the same session and the same per-file key: already-received chunks are skipped, not re-sent.
uploading.p9: A chunk that does arrive twice is rejected early and cheaply: the server recognizes it by index before it reads the body, so a duplicate multi-MB chunk is turned away without being uploaded again, and never stored twice.
uploading.p10: A chunk is first staged on the server, then a background worker pushes it to your storage platform. Completion is reported once every chunk has been received; durability on the platform follows immediately after.
uploading.p13: A partial upload survives a page reload. As soon as a session exists, the client saves a small pointer to it (session id, file identity, chunk layout), never the key. Re-add the same file after a refresh and the client re-derives the file’s key from the server-stored wrapped key plus your passphrase, then picks up from the chunks already received. The raw key is never written to disk, so this stays zero-knowledge.
uploading.p14: Even with no local pointer at all: a different device, a cleared browser, a fresh session : resume still works, because the server is the source of truth. When you start an upload for a file that already has an active session (matched by its content hash and size), the server hands that session back instead of creating a duplicate, pinned to its original storage platform. The client adopts it and continues.
uploading.p15: A browser can’t re-read a file’s bytes on its own after a reload, so resuming means re-selecting the same file. The client checks the name and size match the pending session before continuing: picking the wrong file would corrupt the result, so a mismatch is refused.
uploading.a16: You’ll be asked to re-pick the file
uploading.p18: Interrupted uploads don’t just vanish. An unfinished uploads panel lists every session you started but never finished: showing the filename, size, the storage platform it was headed to, how far it got, and when it expires. Each one gives you two choices:
uploading.p19: Resume. Re-select the file and the upload continues from the server’s already-received chunks, on its original platform.
uploading.p20: Discard. Cancel the session and delete its staged chunks server-side : the deliberate “give up” path.
uploading.p21: Unfinished uploads are kept for 7 days, then removed automatically, long enough that an interrupted multi-GB upload can wait for you to get back to a good connection.
uploading.p23: Pausing is not cancelling. A pause stops the transfer at three layers at once: the loop stops launching new chunks, chunks that already finished encrypting check the paused state before touching the network, and any transfer already on the wire is aborted, while leaving the server session and the resume context intact. Resume simply continues from where it stopped. Cancel is the opposite: it tears down the session and deletes staged data, so it can’t be resumed.
uploading.p24: Clearing an upload from the transfer dock is non-destructive: it stops the local run but leaves the server session alive, so the upload reappears under unfinished uploads. Only an explicit Cancel/Discard throws the staged data away.
uploading.a25: Dismissing a row keeps it recoverable
uploading.p26: The percentage you see is honest. Progress is measured in real bytes sent, completed chunks count their full size, and a chunk still in flight contributes its sent bytes at a slight discount, since reaching the server isn’t the same as being confirmed. The displayed number is monotonic: it never runs backwards, so a retried or aborted chunk can’t make the bar dip. Hashing a large file before upload shows in the stage label rather than eating into the bar, and a resume starts the bar at its true position instead of snapping to zero.
uploading.p28: zcrypt supports two upload paths, chosen automatically per platform:
uploading.p29: Relay (default). Chunks go to the zcrypt server, which stages them and forwards them to the platform. This works for every backend and keeps the client’s job simple.
uploading.p30: Direct / presigned. For Hugging Face, which uses Git LFS, the server hands back a presigned URL and the client uploads the chunk straight to LFS storage, bypassing the server relay. This removes the double hop and is well suited to large files. The directly-uploaded chunks are then confirmed and committed in a single batch.
uploading.p31: The chunk is already encrypted before it leaves your device, so neither path, nor the presigned storage URL, ever handles readable data.
uploading.p34: Multiple files and multiple chunks upload in parallel for speed, but concurrency is capped on both ends. The client limits how many transfers run at once based on your device, and the server bounds concurrent chunk processing: including a small per-repository limit, since some platforms create one commit per file and concurrent commits to the same repo would otherwise collide. The result is fast uploads without overwhelming memory or the platform’s API.
uploading.p35: Dropping a batch of files from a phone works the same way. A batch of many small files uploads several at a time rather than strictly one-by-one, and the most expensive setup steps (deriving your key and spinning up the encryption workers) are done once per batch and shared across every file, so a folder of photos doesn’t pay that cost dozens of times over.
uploading.p37: An upload lands in the folder you are currently viewing: the file is created directly in that folder rather than dropped at the root and moved afterward.
uploading.p38: If the destination is a <l1>password-protected folder</l1>, the upload is wrapped under that folder’s password instead of your vault passphrase, so the file is sealed to the folder from the moment it is stored. (This is also why resuming a protected-folder upload requires that folder to be unlocked, the remaining chunks must be encrypted with the same key as the ones already sent.)
uploading.p39: As for which storage a file lands on: when the platform picker is on Auto, the server resolves the destination for you (Telegram first), and a resume always stays on the session’s original platform. See Platform adapters for how that routing works.

uploading.title: Uploading
uploading.description: Files are compressed, encrypted, and chunked on your device, then streamed to your storage one chunk at a time. The upload survives refreshes, drops, and even a switch to another device, and it lands exactly where you are in your drive.

viewing-files.p1: Before you even open a file, the grid shows you what it is. Images and videos get a real thumbnail (a small preview of the file itself) and everything else gets a crisp, macOS-style type icon: a colored glyph and label (Document, Image, Video, Audio, Spreadsheet, Code, Archive, and so on) on a little page tile.
viewing-files.p2: Generated on your device. A thumbnail is built by decrypting the file in your browser, drawing it to a canvas, and encoding a tiny preview, the same zero-knowledge path as the viewer. For a video, zcrypt grabs a frame a little way in so you get a representative still rather than a black opening frame.
viewing-files.p3: Lazy and cached. Each preview is generated the first time its card comes into view, then cached locally on your device, so it appears instantly next time without decrypting the file again.
viewing-files.p4: Icons for the rest. Files that aren’t images or video, and very large files that aren’t worth decrypting just for a preview, fall back to their type icon instead.
viewing-files.p5: Thumbnails are made from the decrypted file in your browser and kept only in your browser’s local cache. They are never uploaded, your storage platform and our servers only ever hold the encrypted chunks.
viewing-files.p8: Click a file to open the full-screen viewer, an overlay that renders the file in place. It is the quickest way to check a document, scrub a video, or skim a folder of images without saving anything to disk.
viewing-files.p10: The viewer handles a wide range of formats directly in the browser:
viewing-files.p18: HTML previews are sanitized and have scripting disabled before they are shown, so opening an HTML file can't run code or phone home from inside your vault.
viewing-files.p21: Previewing is zero-knowledge. zcrypt fetches the encrypted chunks, then decrypts and decompresses them in your browser just long enough to render the preview. The plaintext stays local. It is never written to your storage platform and never sent to our servers.
viewing-files.p23: Once open, the viewer steps through the whole folder. Move prev/next across files, watch the counter track your position, and go fullscreen for media. Everything is reachable from the keyboard:
viewing-files.p30: For the complete list of supported formats and how each renderer works, see <l1>File viewers</l1>.
viewing-files.title: Viewing & previewing files
viewing-files.description: Open a file to read or watch it right in the browser, no download, no plaintext leaving your device.

toc.remember: Keep me unlocked on this device

web-app.p1: zcrypt works in any modern browser on desktop or mobile. There is nothing to install. All encryption and decryption happen on your device using the Web Crypto API, so your files are sealed and opened locally and the server only ever handles ciphertext.
web-app.p3: zcrypt uses one passphrase to unlock everything for a session. Rather than prompting you per file or per action, the app shows a single lock indicator, a small pill in the interface, and a single unlock modal. Enter your vault passphrase once and the whole vault opens for that session.
web-app.p4: Locked: folder names show as placeholders and nothing can be decrypted. The pill invites you to unlock.
web-app.p5: Unlocked: your passphrase is held in memory for the session so previews, downloads, and search work without re-prompting.
web-app.p6: By default a session unlock lasts 15 minutes of activity and then auto-locks, dropping the passphrase and any decrypted data from memory.
web-app.p7: Folders you protect with their own password are the one exception: they ask for that folder's password the first time you open them in a session. See <l1>per-folder encryption</l1>.
web-app.p9: On a device that's yours, you can opt in to keep me unlocked on this device so a page reload doesn't make you re-enter your passphrase. This is convenience with real engineering behind it, not a plaintext shortcut.
web-app.p10: Your passphrase is encrypted at rest and stored in IndexedDB, never in localStorage and never as plaintext.
web-app.p11: It's encrypted with an AES-GCM key that is non-extractable: the browser can use the key to decrypt but its raw bytes can never be read back out, even by zcrypt's own code.
web-app.p12: The passphrase never leaves your device and is never sent to the server: turning this on changes nothing about what the server can see.
web-app.p13: Locking the vault, or switching the option off, wipes the on-device copy so a later reload stays locked.
web-app.p14: It is off by default. While it is on, anyone who can use this browser profile can open your vault, because the key sits on the same device as the ciphertext. Only turn it on for a device nobody else uses.
web-app.p15: Staying unlocked on a device is strictly your opt-in choice. The non-extractable key makes it far safer than a stored plaintext string, but it is not a defense against malware or a hostile script already running in your browser: such code could ask the key to decrypt. Leave it off on shared or untrusted machines.
web-app.a17: Keep me unlocked on this device
web-app.p18: Uploads and downloads keep running while you work in other tabs. With your permission, zcrypt can post a browser notification when a transfer finishes, so you don't have to babysit a long job. Notifications are shown only while the zcrypt tab is in the background (when it's focused, the in-app progress UI is enough) and they request permission only when there's something worth telling you.
web-app.p19: Notifications are entirely local to your browser and purely informational. Denying the permission has no effect on transfers; you just won't get the desktop pop-up.

zero-knowledge.p1: Zero-knowledge means the service can store and serve your data without ever being able to read it. Your file contents are encrypted on your device with keys derived from a passphrase we never receive. Even with full administrative access to the database and storage, we cannot reconstruct your files, and neither can anyone who compels us to hand over what we have.
zero-knowledge.p2: It does not mean we store nothing. Running a usable drive requires some metadata , sizes, chunk counts, timestamps. The honest version of the claim is: encrypted content stays encrypted, and we are explicit about every piece of metadata that is not.
zero-knowledge.p4: Here is the full inventory of what lands in our database for a typical file and its folder.
zero-knowledge.p10: AES-256-GCM ciphertext; live on your storage backend, not our DB
zero-knowledge.p13: The per-file key, encrypted under your passphrase-derived KEK
zero-knowledge.p16: Folder names are encrypted client-side; we store only ciphertext
zero-knowledge.p19: Published so others can share to you; a public key reveals nothing sensitive
zero-knowledge.p22: X25519 sharing key, encrypted under your passphrase-derived key
zero-knowledge.p25: A shared-space key sealed to each member's public key; only they can open it
zero-knowledge.p28: Original, compressed, and encrypted sizes; number of chunks
zero-knowledge.p31: Integrity digests; reveal nothing about plaintext
zero-knowledge.p34: New names are encrypted client-side. Older files may keep a plaintext name until the web app re-seals it. See below
zero-knowledge.p37: Email, bcrypt password hash, and audit events (IP, user-agent, type)
zero-knowledge.p38: Security events (logins, folder deletions, key changes) are recorded with a coarsened IP address (/24 for IPv4, /48 for IPv6), user-agent, and event type so you and we can spot abuse. These records never contain key material, passphrases, or plaintext file contents.
zero-knowledge.p41: Your passphrase. It is never transmitted and never stored, not even as a hash. It exists only in your device's memory while your vault is unlocked.
zero-knowledge.p42: Your encryption keys. The CEK and the passphrase-derived KEK are computed and used entirely client-side.
zero-knowledge.p43: Your plaintext file contents. The server only ever handles already-encrypted chunks.
zero-knowledge.p44: Your folder names. These are encrypted on your device before upload.
zero-knowledge.p45: Your X25519 private key. The private half of your sharing keypair is wrapped under your passphrase before it is stored; we hold only ciphertext we cannot open.
zero-knowledge.p46: Shared-space keys. When you share, the key is sealed to the recipient's public key; only their private key can open it, never the server. See below.
zero-knowledge.p47: Any per-folder password. A protected folder is verified locally; the password never reaches us. See per-folder encryption.
zero-knowledge.p48: An attacker with our entire database walks away with ciphertext blobs, wrapped keys they cannot unwrap, bcrypt password hashes, and size metadata. They cannot decrypt a single file. A subpoena produces the same useless set: we cannot comply with a demand to read your data because we have no means to.
zero-knowledge.p51: Sharing with another zcrypt user does not open a back door. Every account publishes an X25519 public key to a registry we keep in the clear, while the matching private key is wrapped under that user's passphrase and is opaque to us. To share a space and its files, your device seals the space key to the recipient's public key : an operation only their private key can reverse.
zero-knowledge.p52: We store the sealed grant and the space-wrapped file envelopes, and can read neither. The plaintext space key exists only on members' devices.
zero-knowledge.p53: The server is a directory of public keys and a courier for sealed blobs, never a party to the key exchange itself.
zero-knowledge.p54: Removing a member rotates the space key and re-seals it to whoever remains, so a revoked grant opens nothing.
zero-knowledge.p55: Because we serve the public-key registry, a dishonest server could try to substitute a key it controls. Each key carries a short SHA-256 fingerprint members can compare out of band to catch that. The exact sealed-box construction is in the <l1>encryption model</l1>.
zero-knowledge.a56: Trust the fingerprint, not just the server
zero-knowledge.p58: We will not over-claim here. Folder names are fully encrypted client-side : the database stores only an opaque encrypted_name blob it cannot read. File names are encrypted the same way: every upload must send an opaque encrypted_name (the server refuses uploads without one) and the legacy plaintext original_name column stays empty. That legacy column still exists and can hold plaintext for files uploaded long ago; the web app re-seals those names automatically when you unlock your vault and list your files.
zero-knowledge.p59: Folder structure and folder names are private. A locked vault shows folders as [locked].
zero-knowledge.p60: Older files may still carry a plaintext name in the legacy metadata column until your web app has re-sealed it. New uploads do not.
zero-knowledge.p61: File contents are unaffected. Names are metadata; the bytes inside every file are encrypted regardless.
zero-knowledge.p62: If an older file's name is itself sensitive (for example, it contains a person's name or a case number), unlock your vault in the web app once so the name is re-sealed. The contents are protected either way.
zero-knowledge.p65: There is exactly one surface that is not zero-knowledge, and we would rather you hear it from us. To push and pull encrypted chunks on your behalf, the server has to use your storage-provider credentials (GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, Telegram). Those tokens are encrypted at rest, but not with your passphrase. They are encrypted with a key the server itself can derive.
zero-knowledge.p66: The server holds a single MASTER_KEY and derives a per-user Key Encryption Key from it using HKDF-SHA256.
zero-knowledge.p67: That KEK encrypts your storage-provider tokens with AES-256-GCM before they touch the database, never plaintext at rest.
zero-knowledge.p68: This lets zcrypt act on your storage account, but it does not give the server any ability to read your files: the tokens unlock the repository, and the repository holds only ciphertext.
zero-knowledge.p69: The blast radius is your storage credentials, not your data. Even with your tokens, an attacker reaches encrypted chunks they cannot decrypt without your passphrase. We document this trade-off rather than paper over it. See the <l1>threat model</l1> for where it sits among the risks.

zero-knowledge.title: Zero-knowledge architecture
zero-knowledge.description: Zero-knowledge is a strong claim, so we state it precisely. zcrypt cannot read your file contents or your folder names, and we are equally clear about the metadata it does keep and the single surface that is not zero-knowledge.
zero-knowledge.p77: Other labels are sealed too: timed-vault names, snapshot labels, sync-folder paths, decoy file names, Send and folder-link display names, and Space names and descriptions are sealed on your device and carry an enc1: prefix. Rows saved before sealing shipped stay plaintext until they are saved again.
